activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
story:
Victoria would tell you, if you asked, that she was not superstitious, and that she had not been counting the days since the scholarship deadline, and that the tin of cash her mother sent home every month, the remittance her grandmother called "the envelope," had nothing to do with her poster for the district show. All of this was mostly true, in the way things are true when you say them quickly.

The project was a wheat-paste style poster, printed in halves because the classroom printer only took A4, and it had to look like one seamless image at A2 size. Mr. Liu had left a stack of A3 on the front table with a note that said TAKE WHAT YOU NEED, WHICH IS NOT ALL OF IT, and Victoria took two sheets, which she felt was reasonable, which she would defend as reasonable, though she had also taken a third and put it in her bag, which she preferred not to think about.

She had designed the poster on her laptop at a scale she assumed was right, because her eye was good, everyone said her eye was good, and an eye like that did not need to do arithmetic. Eshaan, who sat by the window and cut his linoleum blocks with surgical patience, leaned over the table and frowned at her screen. "Your two halves don't match," he said. "The top one is taller. Or the bottom one is wider. One of those."

"They match," Victoria said. "It's the screen." But she measured anyway, pressing the ruler flat against the A3 sheet, and the numbers came out wrong in a way that felt personal. Half of 420 was 210; she knew that much. Yet her top half, scaled for a sheet that was 297 by 420, did not line up with the bottom half she had scaled at 297 by 297, like a square, because she had always thought of half a sheet as square. Everyone thought of half a sheet as square. She had been certain of this since she was about six, and being wrong about something she had been certain of since six was like biting foil.

Andreas arrived late, as he did, smelling of the kiln room, and dropped into the seat across from her. He watched her move the ruler back and forth for a while the way you watch someone try to open a door that says push. Then he said, "That's ISO 216, I think," and she said, "What is," and he said, "The paper. A4 and A3 and all of them. The sides are in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so if you cut a sheet in half you get two sheets the same shape as the one you started with."

Victoria looked at him, then at the ruler, then at him again. "So half of A3 isn't a weird rectangle. It's A4."

"It's A4," Andreas said, already losing interest, rolling a coil of clay between his palms until it went ductile and glossy, which was the state he liked best, soft enough to bend without cracking. "So your top half just needs to be scaled like the bottom half. They're the same shape. Both of them. All of them, all the way down."

She wanted to argue, a little, because arguing was how she checked whether a thing was real. But the numbers were already rearranging themselves in her head, obediently, irritatingly. She rescaled the top half, hit print, and walked the two warm sheets to the light table. They matched. Not almost, not close enough. The seam ran through the middle of her figure's folded hands and vanished, because the proportions were identical, because some committee she would never meet had decided centuries ago, or whenever, that paper should halve into itself forever.

Mr. Liu drifted past on his rounds and paused at the light table, and Victoria braced for a speech, some pronouncement about geometry and design that would incapacitate the whole discovery, turn it into a lesson she'd have to write down. He only looked for a moment. "Nice registration," he said, and moved on toward Eshaan's bench.

Here is what Victoria could not stop wondering, though, walking home with the rolled poster under her arm like a bone: had she really not known, all these years, or had she known and refused to look? Her mother sent money home in an envelope every month and never once explained the arithmetic of it, what it cost, what it bought, and Victoria had never asked, the same way she had never once measured a piece of paper. There were things you scaled by eye because measuring them meant admitting they could be wrong. The poster matched perfectly and she still did not know if the composition was any good. Those were separate facts. She suspected they would stay separate.

At the library the next morning she fed coins into the public printer and ran the file at A4, then, on a last impulse, at A3, just to see. The two versions came out of the tray one after the other, and she laid the small one on the big one by the window, corner to corner, and they matched. Same shape, exactly, one hiding inside the other like a smaller version of the same thought.

A woman at the next carrel glanced over. "What are you doing with those?"

Victoria picked up the small sheet and held it against the window, light coming through both at once. "I'm checking something," she said. "I'm still checking."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
story:
The line at the middle school gymnasius moved slowly, and Mackenzie had plenty of time to reread the sample ballot she'd folded into her jacket pocket so many times the creases were going soft. She had turned eighteen in March, and tonight was the first election she had ever been entitled to vote in, a fact she kept turning over the way she turned over a coin in her palm, checking which side kept landing faceup. Behind her, Lukas was frowning at his phone.

"I don't get it," he said. "It says my registration is inactive. I registered in August."

"Maybe the website is just slow," Mackenzie said, though the line was shortening ahead of them and there would be no time to fix whatever inactive meant.

Lukas had moved here in September from North Dakota, where he'd spent his whole life until his mother's job brought them east. He was in two of her classes and had a way of arguing about river water rights that made even Mr. Kerr sit back and listen. At the check-in table, a volunteer in a knitted vest peered at her screen and told him, gently, that he couldn't vote here without an active registration, and that he might be able to sort it out at the county office by the deadline tomorrow.

"That's not how it works where I'm from," Lukas said, and it came out querulous, which wasn't like him, and he seemed to hear it himself and lower his voice. "North Dakota doesn't have registration at all. It's the only state that doesn't. They abolished it back in 1951. You just show ID at the polls and they check you against the list of who lives there."

"That can't be right," the volunteer said, but a second volunteer, older, looked up and said, "No, he's right. I remember that from a training. We're the ones with the paperwork." She found a provisional form and walked Lukas to a clipboard at the end of the table, telling him it might count, it might not, but he should fill it out anyway, and Mackenzie watched him sit down with the pen like a man handed an apology that didn't quite fit.

Her own check-in took forty seconds. Name, address, signature, a ballot in a gray folder, and then a booth with a felt-tip pen on a string. Alone behind the little canvas screen, she took out the ballot and found that the deciding she'd done over three weeks of reading hadn't decided anything. Her father texted every few days about the county commission race, forwarding the campaign's emails with subject lines in capital letters, and some part of her felt that voting his way was a kind of patrimony, something handed down that you accepted unless you had a better reason than mood. But she'd also spent an evening on the phone with Anton, who worked at the food bank and talked about which commissioner had actually shown up when the freezer failed, and his account lined up with nothing her father forwarded.

She had promised her father she'd think for herself, which was easy to promise and turned out to be the hard part, because thinking for yourself still meant thinking with the voices you'd been given. She marked the state races quickly, the ones she'd researched, and then sat with the county commission contest until the pen began to dry at its tip and she had to scribble on the corner of the folder to bring it back. Earlier that week she'd written a letter to her grandmother, who couldn't get to the polls anymore, and her grandmother had written back in blue ink: "I voted for the school bonds in 1974 and your grandfather didn't speak to me for a week, and I have never once regretted the vote, only the week." Mackenzie had taped the letter above her desk, and she thought of it now, of two people in one kitchen holding different opinions and still passing each other the salt.

She filled in the oval beside the candidate Anton had described, then held the ballot at arm's length, checking it the way you check a signature, as if her hand might know something her head hadn't settled. It was possible she was wrong. It was possible her father was wrong in the other direction, and neither of them would know for years, maybe ever. She fed the ballot into the machine, heard it click and whir, and watched the counter tick upward by one, a small mechanical event that seemed to presage nothing and everything.

Outside, Lukas was waiting on the steps with his provisional receipt in his hand, folded into eighths. "So did you do it?" he asked.

"I did it. Did you?"

"Maybe," he said. "They'll tell me in ten days. Ten days to find out if I voted." He laughed, then stopped laughing. "First election, and I might not even count."

"You'll count next time," Mackenzie said, and then, because it sounded too much like a consolation, she added, "And now you know more about registration than anyone I've ever met." He held the door of the gymnasium open for an older woman coming up the steps with a cane, and the two of them stood there a moment longer in the cold, watching the line inside grow and shrink under the fluorescent lights.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The line outside the church gymnasium moved slowly, and Brayden had time to regret coming before he reached the door. He was eighteen and three weeks, old enough that his mother had put the voter card on the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lobster, young enough that he still wasn't sure he deserved the pen they would hand him. Behind him, Christian was narrating the parking lot. "That guy's been sitting in his truck for ten minutes," Christian said. "Rehearsing, probably. His whole ballot speech."

"Maybe he's just cold."

"Nobody sits in a truck in the cold rehearsing nothing." Christian had voted in the advance polls already, mostly, Brayden suspected, so that he could spend election day being superior about it. He fell into step beside Brayden now with the ease of someone who had habituated himself to Brayden's silences over eleven years of shared bus seats and group projects neither of them had wanted.

Inside, a woman with a lanyard found Brayden's name in a binder and slid a ballot across the table. Beside him, a girl he half recognized from chemistry, Vera, was showing her registration to a second worker, an older man with reading glasses pushed up into his hair. "First time," she said, and Brayden heard the small pride in it, the same pride he had swallowed on the walk over.

"Mine too," Brayden said.

Vera turned. "Do you know how long people our age have even been allowed to do this? I asked my grandfather and he said when he was our age he couldn't." She looked at the worker, who smiled and shook his head, offering nothing.

"I read it in the library when I was researching my civics essay," Brayden said. "Canada lowered the federal voting age from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970. So it's not even sixty years. My dad's older than that." He heard how it sounded, like showing off, and tried to soften it. "I only remember because it was the last fact on my notecard."

Vera had stopped moving toward the booth. "My grandfather turned twenty-one the year after," she said. "He missed one election by a year. He talks about it like it's the funniest thing that ever happened to him, but I don't think it's funny to him at all." She said it lightly, the way people set down something heavy and then walk away from it.

Brayden took his ballot to the booth and stood with the pencil hovering. His mother wanted him to vote a certain way; she had said so at dinner twice, in the tone she used for things that were not actually requests. Christian wanted him to vote another way and had texted him a list of reasons at midnight, numbered, with sources. Brayden had read both arguments carefully, partly to please them and partly because he could not yet tell the difference between wanting to be informed and wanting to be finished. The incipient certainty he had felt on the bus, that morning feeling of finally having an opinion, had thinned the way morning fog does. There was no etiology he could point to for his own hesitation, no single cause; there was only his mother's kitchen and Christian's texts and Vera's grandfather missing an election by a year, all of it mixed into a decision that would take four seconds to mark and then belong to him forever.

He thought about the man in the truck. Rehearsing, Christian had said, and Brayden had defended him, but standing in the booth he understood the impulse. He marked the ballot, and it was not exactly a compromise between his mother and Christian, though it borrowed from both, and it was not exactly conviction either. It was the closest thing to a considered position he could build out of what he knew, with room left over for everything he didn't. That unsettled part he would keep, he decided, the way you keep a receipt for something you might still return.

He fed the ballot into the box and heard it drop. Outside, the sky had gone the grey of late afternoon, and Christian was waiting on the church steps with two coffees from the place across the road.

"Even traded," Christian said, holding one out.

"I can't tell you who I voted for."

"Obviously. That's the whole point." Christian looked wounded anyway, briefly, and then shrugged and drank his own coffee.

Vera came out behind them, stuffing her registration card into her jacket pocket, and paused on the bottom step. "My grandfather's going to ask me if it felt important," she said. "I'm going to tell him it felt like everything and nothing at the same time." She pulled her hood up and walked toward the bus stop, and Brayden watched her go, the coffee going warm in his hand.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Gar Alperovitz argued in Atomic Diplomacy (1965) that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union.
story:
The bus from campus let them off at the gate of the veterans' memorial just after ten, and Addison folded the photocopied pages into her jacket pocket before the wind could take them. One page was an excerpt from Gar Alperovitz's Atomic Diplomacy, published in 1965, arguing that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. The other was from a historian who called that argument revisionist nonsense, a Cold War story read backwards into a hot war. Ms. Moose, their seminar instructor, had assigned both without comment and told them to meet the evidence at the memorial itself, where the state kept its own version of things.

Jessa had claimed the anti-Alperovitz side before the bus even finished boarding. "Four months of conventional bombing already burned Tokyo to the ground," she said on the walk up the gravel path. "The bombs were just a bigger version of what was already happening. Last act of the Second World War, not a chess move against Stalin." Fatima, walking between them with her hands in her sleeves against the cold, demurred. "You can hold that and still ask why it happened when it happened," she said quietly, and Addison thought that was the most honest sentence anyone had produced all morning.

Inside the museum wing, the exhibit on 1945 ran along a single long wall. Addison moved slowly, reading every placard, copying phrases into her notebook. The text mentioned the planned invasion of Kyushu, the projected casualties, the ultimatum at Potsdam. It mentioned the Soviet entry into the war on August 8th in a single sentence, low on the panel, almost an afterthought. She stood in front of that sentence for a long time. "This is the thing," she said to Fatima, not loudly. "If you believe the bombs ended the war, the Soviets are a footnote. If you believe Alperovitz, that footnote is the whole story, and somebody chose to make it small."

Jessa drifted back from the gift shop with three postcards and an expression of pure ennui, the boredom of someone who has decided the question is settled. "You're both going to stand there reading the wall until lunch," she said. "It's a memorial, not a courtroom." But she stayed anyway, hovering at Addison's shoulder, and when Addison tapped the glass over a photograph of the Potsdam delegation, Jessa leaned in despite herself. "Truman looks tired," Jessa said. "That's not an argument, obviously." "It's not," Addison agreed, "but look at the dates on the caption. He was in the room with Stalin while the test results were coming in from New Mexico. The wall doesn't say what he knew and when. Alperovitz says the diplomacy around the bomb matters more than the wall admits."

They argued on the terrace afterward, over sandwiches Fatima had wrapped in wax paper and divided into three unequal portions because she knew Jessa always forgot food. Jessa called the Alperovitz reading bellicose in reverse, turning every American decision into an act of aggression against an ally. Addison pushed back, but carefully, the way she had learned to push in Ms. Moose's seminar, testing the idea rather than the friend. "He's not saying the bombs didn't end the war," she said. "He's saying the word 'partly' does a lot of work. Partly to intimidate the Soviets. Two motives can sit in the same decision. People are like that." Fatima, crumbs on her knee, said, "Then the question is which motive the evidence can actually carry, and I don't think this wall carries either one. It carries grief. That's a different document."

Addison wrote that down too. In her notebook she made two columns, one headed "ends the war" and one headed "intimidates the USSR," and under each she listed what the memorial had offered and what it had not. The invasion plans went in the left column. The Soviet entry into the war, the timing, the silence about what Truman hoped the bomb would do to Stalin's posture in Eastern Europe, those went in the right, though the right column felt thinner, built mostly from the excerpt in her pocket and the wall's omissions rather than from anything the wall said. She could not make the two columns agree, and she noticed that she did not want them to agree, that the discomfort of holding both felt more truthful than either one alone.

On the bus back, Jessa fell asleep against the window and Fatima transferred her own scarf, without waking her, from her bag to Jessa's shoulders. Addison looked out at the highway barriers sliding past and thought about Ms. Moose, who would ask them on Monday not for a verdict but for a weighing. She had one, half-formed: that the bombs could be the last act of one war and the first act of another at the same time, and that the memorial, built to mourn, could not be expected to say so. What she did not have was proof, and she underlined the gap in her notebook and wrote beside it, "ask about the archives." The bus hissed at a red light, and Fatima asked if she was going to be all right giving up certainty. Addison zipped the notebook shut and said, "I'm going to be all right giving it a grade."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
Logan had inherited the garage the week his brother left for basic training, and the first thing he did was wheel the workbench against the far wall and spread a drop cloth over the oil stains. On the bench he laid out his mother's old brushes, a jar of water, and six tubes of acrylic he'd bought with his graduation money. The plan was a painting for Cora, something for the blank wall above her dorm bed, and he had promised it to her by Sunday. He had promised things before, though, and he was trying not to think about the summer after sophomore year, when he'd abandoned a whole series of sketches for her birthday and shown up with nothing but an apology.

He sketched the composition in pencil first: the water tower behind the school, the train tracks cutting east, a sky he decided would be yellow-gray rather than blue because blue felt like a lie about that place. He was, he admitted to himself, being a little revisionist about his own hometown, editing out the parts that had been merely boring and keeping the parts that looked meaningful in retrospect. Ms. Lindqvist would have called him on it. In her seminar last spring she'd warned them not to historicize their memories, not to treat seventeen as if it were already an era with a fixed character, and he'd argued with her for half a period about whether that was even possible. He still wasn't sure it was. He knew only that the painting was turning out better when he let it be one afternoon instead of a verdict.

He worked for two hours, thinning the paint with water when he wanted the tracks to bleed into the gravel, letting it sit thick where the tower needed weight. Around noon his phone buzzed, and Bentley was outside in his car with two sandwiches and no plans, as usual. Logan set his brushes across the jar, an act that took one second and that he would think about later with a specific, private irritation, and went out to sit on the driveway with his shoes in the grass.

They ate and argued about whether their history teacher had been fair to the class's valedictorian, and Bentley was ebullient on the subject, gesturing with the second half of his sandwich, insisting the whole grading system was a scam. Logan defended the system without believing in it much, which was a habit of his he noticed only afterward. When Bentley finally pulled away, forty minutes had gone. In the garage, the brushes had gone hard. The one he'd been using for the sky stood stiff as a spike, its bristles fused into a single gray-blue blade, and when he held it under the tap the water ran off it without doing anything at all.

He swore, quietly, and stood there turning the ruined brush in his hand. He tried hot water. He tried working the bristles with his thumbnail. Nothing moved. The paint on the palette had skinned over too, a rubbery film he could peel off in one piece like something from a pond. So that was the nature of what he was working with: it obeyed you completely while it was wet, and then, without ceremony, it stopped.

He was still scrubbing when Cora texted to ask how it was going, and he sent her a photo of the brush without commentary. She replied within a minute. "You left them out? Acrylic is water-based while it's wet. Once it dries, it's water-resistant. It's basically plastic now." He read it twice, sitting on an overturned milk crate, the wet brush dripping a line onto the concrete. He had half a mind to be defensive, to point out that she had never once cleaned a brush in her life, that her contribution to his last project had been enthusiastic commentary from a lawn chair. But she wasn't wrong, and being wrong in the company of someone who knew felt different from being wrong alone.

He texted back that he'd lost the sky brush and she'd owe him a sandwich. Then he got the good brushes, the two his mother had left in the cabinet under the sink, and set a timer on his phone this time, ten minutes, so that the argument with Bentley would have to happen faster or not at all. He worked through the afternoon in short sessions, washing the brushes at each interval, keeping the paint damp, and the yellow-gray sky went on in layers that he could still change while they were wet. The tower took until dusk. He stepped back from it and found that he'd left the tracks unfinished, running off the bottom edge into nothing, and he stood there deciding whether that was a cop-out or the truest part of the whole thing.

He picked up the ruined brush, the stiff one, and turned it over in his hand. Then he dipped a fresh brush in water and started on the tracks.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Sugar bloom is a dry, gritty white coating caused when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries.
story:
The kitchen of the Marisol had gone quiet after the dinner rush, and Justin stood at the steel counter with a slab of dark chocolate and a palette knife, trying to hold his mind steady along with the temperature of the bowl. Mr. Pereira, the pastry chef, had shown him once and only once: melt, cool, reheat, test on the lip of the counter. A streak that set dull meant failure; a streak that set with a snap and a shine meant he had it. Justin had failed three times in two evenings. He wanted tonight to be different, mostly because Elle had promised to come by after her shift bussing tables, and because Suri had already told him, in her laconic way, that watching him fail again was better entertainment than anything on her phone.

"Stop hovering," he said, though Suri was six feet away, leaning on the reach-in with her apron still on.

"I'm not hovering. I'm observing." She peeled a clementine. "There's a difference."

The chocolate moved like something alive, thickening as it cooled, loosening as he warmed it again over the water bath. He had spent the bus ride home the night before reading about tempering on his phone, half listening to his mother talk about the orientation paperwork for the college he would start in the fall. The two threads had tangled in his head. The chemistry teacher at school had tried for four years to inculcate the idea that matter follows rules, that if you understood the rules you could predict what would happen, and Justin had mostly resisted, because in his experience rules were things adults used to make you predictable. But the chocolate obeyed something. The cocoa butter wanted one crystal form and not another, and whether it chose rightly depended on him.

He streaked the counter. Waited. Touched it. It set fast and smooth, and when he tapped it with the knife it broke with a clean, glassy sound.

"Finally," Suri said, straightening up.

He poured the tempered chocolate into the molds Elle had brought from the dining room, taps and shells she'd been saving from a party order that had cancelled. He scraped the excess, turned the molds over the bowl, and set them on a tray. Then he made his mistake. The walk-in was right there, humming, cold, and he was impatient, so he slid the tray onto its shelf and shut the heavy door, congratulating himself on speed.

Elle came in through the swinging door with her jacket already on. "Are they done? Suri texted me a video of your snap. That was so satisfying." She opened the walk-in before he could say anything, brought the tray out into the warm, steam-heavy air of the kitchen, and the three of them stood looking at it. Within minutes the chocolates had gone cloudy, a dry white powder creeping across the tops like frost.

"No," Justin said. He picked one up. The surface felt gritty under his thumb, rough where it should have been slick.

"That's sugar bloom," Elle said, and he looked at her. "My aunt's candy shop. Anything we took out of the fridge on a humid day turned powdery like that. The moisture gets on the surface, the sugar dissolves, and then it dries all gritty again." She said it lightly, not lecturing, the way she said most things, and set the chocolate back on the tray.

Justin stood there feeling the two halves of the evening, the good streak and the ruined tray, refuse to fit together. He had wanted to believe that tempering was the whole secret, that one perfect snap meant mastery, and it plainly wasn't. He had been treating the kitchen like the contrivance he'd always suspected school was, a machine for producing a single right answer, when really the chocolate answered to everything around it, the cold he had imposed and the humid air he had let in. "So it was the fridge," he said. "I did that."

"You did that," Suri agreed, cheerful about it.

"The book says let them set at room temperature."

"The book says a lot of things."

Mr. Pereira came through from the pastry station drying his hands, glanced at the tray, and raised an eyebrow at Justin without comment. Justin scraped the molds clean back into the bowl, and the chocolate went onto the water bath again to melt, to cool, to be brought back. Elle pulled a stool up to the counter without asking. Suri threw her clementine peel in the compost and stayed.

"There's enough for another batch," Justin said, and tilted the bowl toward the light.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
Eva's grandmother had died eleven days before, and on the twelfth day Eva stood in the family kitchen with flour on her forearms and the oven ticking as it heated. The recipe card was propped against the sugar canister, the handwriting slanting and impatient, and the dough was recalcitrant, crumbling whenever Eva pressed it toward the shape the card demanded. Her mother was at work. The kitchen smelled of butter and cold lemon, because the neighbor, Mr. Wilson, had left a bag of lemons on the porch that morning with a note that said only, For the biscuits.

Eva had started the biscuits because she wanted the biscuits, the specific sandy ones with the jam thumbprint, and because starting them felt like something a functioning person would do. Halfway through, her phone buzzed. Aliza had sent a picture of a dog wearing a rain bonnet, and Eva had laughed, out loud, alone, a real laugh, and then had stood very still with the spoon in her hand. Eleven days. She put the phone face down on the counter and picked the dough back up, and it crumbled again.

Chad texted next. Movie tonight? he wrote. The old one with the stolen bus, the one they had seen four times. Eva typed maybe and deleted it, typed I can't and deleted that too. Her grandmother had been dead eleven days and Eva had laughed at a dog in a bonnet and now she was considering a comedy, and somewhere in her chest a small court had convened, one that seemed ready to impugn the honesty of every pleasant feeling she had. She said so to Aliza when Aliza showed up at four with her backpack and no explanation, the way she sometimes did.

"You look like the dough," Aliza said, nodding at the bowl. "Refusing to cooperate."

"I laughed at your dog picture," Eva said. "This morning. And it was funny, and I laughed, and then I felt like I'd left the funeral early." She wiped her hands on the towel. "Chad wants to go tonight. The bus movie."

"Go to the bus movie."

"It's been a week and a half."

Aliza sat on the counter, which Eva's mother prohibited and Eva's grandmother had encouraged, and took a lemon from Mr. Wilson's bag and turned it over. "We just did a psych unit on this," she said. "Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, the dual process model. Grieving people move back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life. Not one direction. Back and forth."

"So I'm allowed to laugh."

"You're not even allowed. You just do it. The swinging is the thing, not a detente you have to hold." She squeezed the lemon lightly, sniffed her fingers, made a face. "Also I think these are older than our friendship."

Eva looked at the recipe card. It did not say anything about swings or directions. It said 250 grams, cold butter, don't overwork it, and Eva had been overworking it for an hour, which was probably why it kept coming apart in her hands. She had been doing the same thing to the day itself, pressing it toward a single proper shape. She added a splash of milk, gathered the dough gently instead of firmly, and it held.

They rolled it out and pressed thumbprints and filled them with the last of the apricot jam, and Eva said she would text Chad yes, and then said she might still cry during the previews, and then said maybe she would cry during the funny part too, and Aliza said that was allowed by nobody in particular and therefore by everyone. The oven ticked. The phone buzzed on the counter with Chad's reply, three exclamation points and a picture of the bus.

Mr. Wilson's lemons went into the glaze instead of the biscuits, an improvisation the card had not authorized, and when the timer rang, Eva pulled the tray out and set it on the rack to cool. She ate the first one standing up, burnt thumb and all, still in her flour-dusted shirt. "They're close," she said. "Not right yet."

"Try more butter next time," Aliza said.

"Next time," Eva said, and reached for the phone.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
story:
Kaylee had read about it in a photocopied chapter Ms. Fischer left on the back table, the one nobody was supposed to take home: in a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. She had taken it home anyway. Now she was standing at lane eleven in rented shoes two sizes wrong, watching a boy named Vincenzo enter her name into the scoreboard, and she could not stop thinking about posture.

"You put the extra L in," she said.

"That's how you spell it."

"That's one way how you spell it."

He laughed and corrected it. Vincenzo was in her chemistry class, had asked her out on Tuesday with a noncommittal shrug that she had spent three days interpreting, and now here he was, wearing what was clearly his good shirt, the collar pressed flat. She picked up the eight-pound ball because it was blue, not because it was right for her, which Abhijot had told her last week was, quote, her whole personality in one decision. Abhijot thought she overthought things. Abhijot was probably right, and also, Abhijot had once gotten lost in a parking garage for forty minutes, so his opinions carried a discount.

Her first ball slid into the gutter. The second knocked over four pins, and she turned around fast to catch Vincenzo's reaction, some gesture she could read. He gave her a thumbs up. She had wanted more than a thumbs up. On the bench, waiting for his turn, she sat with her elbows on her knees, chin in her hands, and watched him loft the ball out so far it landed with a crack. Two pins.

"Beginner's luck is on your side," she said. "Mine ran out in the womb."

"Nobody's born bowling."

"Vincenzo. Some people are absolutely born bowling."

He came back and sat down, and this was the part she noticed: he sat with his elbows on his knees, chin in his hands. Exactly. Same angle, same dropped shoulders. She felt something in her chest go warm and then immediately suspicious, in that order, like a sprinkler coming on over a fire she hadn't confirmed yet.

There was a boy before him, Marcus, from her old school, who had copied everything she did for two months, her slang, her order at the coffee place, the way she said "honestly" before lying. She'd found it charming then, flattering, evidence of gravity. When he dumped her by text she learned the word for it from a rant online: affectation, a borrowed self worn like a costume. She had promised herself she'd never mistake copying for closeness again. But the chapter said the mimicry in the study was quiet, unnoticed. Vincenzo wasn't performing anything. He didn't know he was doing it. She didn't know if that made it more honest or less, whether a thing you can't help is more yours than a thing you choose.

She tested it, and she was a little ashamed of the test. She crossed her ankles, left over right, and looked at the score screen, not at him. She counted a slow fifteen in her head. His ankles crossed, left over right.

"So my friend Abhijot claims you can't get a real strike on a house ball because they're weighted wrong," she said, arms folded now, testing again. "Is that true or is he indemnifying his six-pin average?"

"He's covering for himself, one hundred percent."

His arms folded. She uncrossed hers. A beat later, his unfolded too, reaching for his drink.

It was real, then, whatever real meant here. He was matching her without knowing it, and the study said the liking ran from the person being copied toward the copier, which meant he should be the one feeling warmer, and which meant, if she wanted to be strategic about a first date, which she refused to be, or mostly refused, she could lean forward when he talked and let the science work for her like everyone else at the party who didn't know they were at a party. That felt like cheating. It also felt like not cheating, since he was doing it to her too, without knowing, which meant nobody was guilty or everybody was, a tie, the bowling equivalent of a split.

Her turn came. She picked the blue ball, walked up, and thought, absurdly, about matching her own delivery to nothing, to no one, just letting the arm do what an arm does. The ball hooked late and took out the corner pin and the one beside it. Nine down.

"Okay," Vincenzo said, standing, "that was luck."

"That was nine pins of skill and one of grace."

"You want to get food after? There's a place that does wings till midnight."

She looked at him, hands in his pockets now because her hands had been in her pockets a second before, or maybe his were there first this time, she honestly couldn't tell anymore which of them had moved first, and she decided she could live with not knowing.

"Wings," she said. "But I'm spelling your name wrong on the scoreboard for the rest of the night."

"Put in both Ls," said Vincenzo, and rolled.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, usually a prime minister, holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a separate popular election.
story:
The community centre had been a legion hall once, and it still felt that way: folding chairs, a spartan kitchen with a kettle nobody had descaled in years, a banner from a bake sale that had never come down. Avery arrived early because the sign-up sheet had warned that latecomers would be assigned sides rather than choosing them, and she had already decided she wanted the parliamentary one. She wrote her name under it in pen and pressed hard enough to score the paper.

Cassius took the presidential side, which surprised no one, since he had spent the entire drive there denigrating the workshop as something for people who couldn't argue without a moderator. Haylee sat between them and took notes on a legal pad even before anything started, which was her way of pretending she wasn't nervous. Ms. Leung, who ran the centre's Thursday programmes, set a timer on the ledge of the whiteboard and said only that they had until four o'clock to run the simulation twice, once under each system.

The exercise began with an election. Cassius campaigned for the presidency with a short speech and won a show of hands, and Haylee recorded it, and Avery watched the parliamentary column of her own notes stay blank. That was when the uneasiness started. In her system, whom exactly was she supposed to elect? She had prepared by reading, and she could recite the differences on paper, but the moment she had to act them out, the machinery went soft in her hands.

"Wait," Haylee said, looking up from the pad. "We haven't picked a prime minister yet. Don't the people get to do that?"

Avery opened her mouth and closed it. Something was pressing at her from the summer, a room and a question she hadn't answered, but it wouldn't surface, and the timer was running, so she improvised. "The legislature picks. Sort of. We vote for members, and the government comes out of that." She heard how vague it sounded, like a person describing a magic trick they'd only seen from the back row.

Cassius pounced, which was Cassius's function in any room. "That's not democracy, that's a consolation prize. My guy got voted in by actual people. Yours got hired." He was grinning, but under the grin he was building a case, and Avery understood with a small cold drop in her stomach that her entire side rested on a fact she couldn't yet state cleanly.

Ms. Leung did not rescue her. She refilled the kettle. That was all, and it was somehow worse than a correction would have been.

Avery asked for a pause, walked to the window bay where the centre kept a shelf of old civics readers beside the lost-and-found box, and found the passage. She read it twice, then a third time, mouthing the words. Then it came back to her, the whole buried afternoon: her grandmother's kitchen in August, a cousin visiting from overseas, spooning sugar into tea and asking why nobody over there had voted directly for the prime minister, and Avery, eighteen and newly proud of her marks, going entirely silent, changing the subject to the garden because she had never actually known. The cousin had let it go. Avery had not, all these months, let herself admit that.

She walked back to the circle, and the room went quiet in the way rooms do when someone returns carrying something.

"In a parliamentary system," she said, "the head of government holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature, not by winning a separate popular election." She said it slowly, once, without ornament, and watched Cassius's grin stall. "So nobody skipped democracy. It's a different door to the same room, or maybe not the same room, I actually don't know that part yet, and I think I'd rather say that than pretend."

Haylee's pen stopped moving. Cassius rubbed the back of his neck and, for once, took a moment before speaking. "So if the legislature stops liking yours," he said, "they can just take them out, no election at all?"

"That part I can't confirm from here," Avery said, tapping the reader against her palm. "What I can confirm is the door."

Ms. Leung set three cups of tea on the table and reset the timer. "Second round," she said. "Ms. Popular-vote wins, you're the legislature now. Show us what confidence looks like when it runs out."

Haylee slid the legal pad toward the middle of the table and drew a single line down the centre of it.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In Canada outside Quebec, a typical paycheque shows deductions for income tax, Canada Pension Plan contributions and Employment Insurance premiums; Quebec uses its own pension and parental insurance plans.
story:
Ava spread the papers across the kitchen table the way other people laid out cards: her pay stub from the hardware store, the receipt from the sandwich shop, and the tax return booklet her mother had left there with a pencil resting in its spine. She had worked eleven shifts since March. Eleven shifts, and her stub said she'd earned four hundred and twelve dollars, of which she was taking home considerably less. That was the part she wanted to understand before she spent the weekend at Deven's.

Deven arrived at four with his own stub folded in his back pocket, because Ava had texted him, bring yours, mine looks robbed. He sat down across from her, helped himself to the last of the grapes without asking, and flattened his paper beside hers. His family had moved to Montreal in January, and he'd almost immediately found work at a grocery store, which he described as hellish but lucrative.

"Okay," Ava said. "Read me your deductions."

He ran his finger down the column. "Income tax. Then this one says QPP. Then QPIP."

"QPP?"

"Quebec Pension Plan, I guess. There's a little Q on everything here."

Ava looked at her own stub. Hers read CPP, Canada Pension Plan, and EI, Employment Insurance, with income tax sitting at the top like a landlord collecting first. She turned the paper sideways as if the angle might reveal something. "So outside Quebec you pay into the Canada Pension Plan and Employment Insurance. In Quebec you've got your own pension thing and your own parental insurance thing instead."

"That's what it looks like," Deven said, chewing a grape. "We still pay income tax. Everyone pays income tax. Nobody escapes that."

"No one but the very brave," said Ava's mother from the counter, where she was slicing an orange into segments and pointedly not helping, which was her way of helping. She set a plate of orange segments between them, which Ava understood as an offering to assuage the shock of the numbers, and went back to the counter.

Deven had been morose all afternoon, though he'd hidden it until the stubs came out. Now it surfaced. "My dad keeps saying I should be saving this money for tuition, and I keep saying it's two hundred dollars, Dad, it's not a tuition, it's a pair of shoes and some groceries." He picked up an orange segment and didn't eat it. "He acts like every dollar I spend is a moral failure."

"He's not an autocrat," Ava said. "He's just scared. There's a difference." She knew this because her own mother had a similar voice, the one that came out around money, and because she'd spent a long time deciding it was fear rather than control, and she still wasn't entirely sure she'd decided correctly. She slid the tax return booklet toward her. "Have you done one of these?"

"Quebec does its own. Of course it does." Deven almost smiled. "Everything there is its own."

She opened the booklet. It was mostly questions about income and lines numbered into the hundreds, and she filled in her eleven shifts' worth of wages with the pencil, then found the line for the tax already taken off her cheques. The numbers were small enough to feel almost friendly. Somewhere in the fine print she read that because she'd earned so little, some of what had been withheld might come back to her, and she sat with that sentence for a moment, because it was the first piece of government paperwork that had ever leaned in her direction.

"Do you think we get the sales tax back too?" Deven asked. He pulled the sandwich shop receipt from under her elbow and pointed at the bottom, where the price of her lunch had grown a tail: GST, plus a provincial tax, nearly fourteen percent in total by the time it was done. On his own crumpled receipt from Montreal the rate was different, smaller, and he tapped it as if presenting evidence.

"I think that one's just gone," Ava said. "I think that's the price of the sandwich."

They added up her receipts, then his, and the difference between the two provinces over one afternoon of eating was forty cents, which felt both meaningless and, somehow, like something worth knowing. Deven stacked the orange segments on his receipt in a little tower. Ava's mother drifted past and set a fresh pile of grapes in front of him without a word, and he said, "Thanks, Mrs. A," and ate the tower.

Ava copied the income tax line from her stub onto the return, checked it twice, and then stopped, pencil hovering, because she couldn't tell whether she was hoping for money back or proud of having paid in at all, and she didn't know if both could be true.

"Mail it yet?" Deven asked.

"Not yet," she said, and folded the stub back into her pocket.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
The binder had been on the shelf between a birdwatching guide and a cookbook titled Everything With Condensed Soup, and Kyle only pulled it down because the wifi at his grandmother's house had been dead since Tuesday. "Leadership Feedback Workshop, 1998," the cover said, in a font that belonged on a laser-tag flyer. His grandfather was in the kitchen pretending the soup hadn't boiled over. Kyle flopped onto the floral couch and read, mostly out of boredom, which was how he'd once learned to juggle and also how he'd once glued his fingers together.

The binder had a section on the Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, which framed feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. "Huh," Kyle said out loud, because the alternative was thinking it silently, and the house was very quiet. There was even a worksheet. Half of it was filled in by some seminar dilettante in blue pen who had apparently believed that attending a workshop was the same as changing. Kyle felt an immediate, undeserved kinship with this stranger.

The reason he cared at all was sitting in his phone: seventeen texts from a group chat about the robotics scrimmage, and one unsent draft to Leia. In the semifinal, she'd been supposed to run the arm checks before their match, hadn't done it, and the gripper had seized up forty seconds in. Since then Kyle had opened the draft four times and written things like "you're lazy" and "whatever, it's fine," which were, he could admit, two kinds of useless. "It's fine" was a lie and "you're lazy" was a verdict. He wanted something in between, and until this moment he'd assumed nothing existed there.

His grandfather came in wiping his hands on a towel that had once been white. "Find anything good, or are you just pretending to read to avoid the dishes?"

"I found your ancient leadership binder. Were you a manager?"

"I ran a hardware store for thirty years, so yes, I was a putative expert on telling people things they didn't want to hear." He sat down in the good chair. "Why, do you have to tell someone something?"

"Leia skipped our robot checks and we lost, and if I text her something mean, Julia will be mad at me, and if I say nothing, I'll be mad at me, and I don't love either option."

"Ah," his grandfather said, and stole the binder, and read for a while, and gave it back, and offered no wisdom whatsoever, which Kyle was beginning to suspect was the wisdom.

He tried it in the margin of his grandmother's grocery list. Situation: before the semifinal. Behavior: you skipped the arm checks and went to look at the other team's robot. Impact: the gripper seized up and Julia had to improvise, and I stood there feeling like a lamp. He crossed out the lamp part. Then he wrote a version that was all impact and no behavior, "you cost us the match," which was somehow worse, an accusation wearing a tie. The worksheet wanted him to instantiate each piece, he noticed, to give one real moment, one real action, one real consequence, not a character assessment dressed as a fact. It was weirdly like debugging. You didn't tell the code it was stupid; you said, at line forty, this variable is empty, and here's what crashed.

He called Leia instead of texting, because the binder had a whole page about tone, and she picked up on the second ring with "If this is about the arm, I already know, Julia sent me a paragraph with bullet points."

"Bullet points are Julia's love language," Kyle said. "Listen, can I try something weird? Before the semifinal, you skipped the arm checks to go scout the other team. The gripper seized up in the match, and Julia had to drive around a dead arm for two minutes, and I didn't say anything at the time, which I think I should have."

There was a pause long enough that he checked whether the call had dropped. "That's it? That's the weird thing?"

"That's the whole thing. It's called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model, it's from some leadership place my grandpa has a binder about, and I didn't want to call you lazy, because you're not, you just didn't do one thing one time."

"Okay," Leia said slowly. "Okay, that's actually better than Julia's bullet points, don't tell her. I skipped the checks because I was convinced the Grippers were running a defense we'd never seen, and I was right, and it didn't matter, because our arm was a paperweight." A drawer clattered on her end. "Can I try it? Situation: today, four o'clock. Behavior: you said 'I should have said something at the time.' Impact: now I know you were holding it, which I did not know, and I would rather know."

Kyle looked over at his grandfather, who was mouthing something that was either "dishes" or a word he wasn't allowed to use. "Impact on me: mild guilt, significant relief."

"Want to come re-run the checks Saturday? I'm bringing donuts as reparations."

"Bring two kinds," Kyle said. "We're a team in crisis."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Many food banks cannot accept home-cooked or opened food, because they cannot check how it was prepared or stored.
story:
Zachary had signed up because the form was due Friday and the box for community service was still empty, and because his mother had said, three times, that it would be good for him to think about someone other than himself. He arrived at the food bank at nine with his backpack still smelling of the coffee he'd spilled on the bus, and stood in the doorway until a man in a lanyard waved him over to a folding table stacked with dented cans.

"You're the Saturday one," the man said. "Mr. Sow. You sort, you date-check, you shelve. Canned goods here, dry goods there, and if you're not sure, you ask before you guess."

Zachary said he could do that. Mr. Sow looked at him a moment longer, as though deciding whether this was true, then handed him a pair of gloves.

Hilary was already at the dry goods shelf, which surprised him, because at school Hilary was the person who argued against assemblies and fund-raisers on the grounds that they were mostly for the people organizing them. She had apparently softened, or else had her own empty box on a form. "Don't put the rice where you're about to put the rice," she said, without looking up. He moved the rice.

Yassine arrived twenty minutes late with a laminated sheet of rules, which he had been given at the door and had read, apparently, in full, walking. "This place has more regulations than the chemistry lab," he said. "Half this sheet is about what we can't take. Did you know that?"

"I haven't read the sheet, Yassine."

"I'm just saying. There's a whole section on donations. It's like being a lawyer, except the pay is worse."

The morning settled into a rhythm. Zachary learned that expired-by-one-day was a conversation with Mr. Sow, expired by more was the bin, and dented-but-sealed went on a special shelf for people who didn't mind dents. He found he liked the sorting, the small decisive judgments of it, and he did not introspect about this, because there was a box of soup in front of him and the box was not going to sort itself.

At half past ten a woman came in with a foil tray held in both hands, the way you'd carry something still warm. She was maybe fifty, in a coat that had seen several winters, and Zachary recognized her before he could place her, and then he placed her: she lived four doors down from him, the house with the flag, and she had once returned their dog when it got out. He hadn't known her name. He still didn't.

"I made a lasagna," she said to Mr. Sow, setting it on the edge of the table. "For the families. My mother's recipe. It's got to go out today, it won't keep."

Mr. Sow's face did something careful. "That's kind of you," he said. "But we can't take home-cooked food. We can't accept it unless it's packaged, unopened. Anything opened or homemade, we have to turn away, because there's no way for us to check how it was prepared or stored." He said it gently, the way you'd say a weather report.

"You're turning away a lasagna."

"I'm turning away a lasagna. I'm sorry."

She stood there with her hands now empty, and the tray sat between them steaming faintly through the foil. Zachary, sorting soup six feet away, stopped sorting soup.

"I could eat it," Yassine said under his breath. "As a service."

"That's not the point," Hilary said, also under her breath.

"There is a point?"

The woman said she understood, she supposed, rules were rules, and picked the tray back up, and it was at the door that Zachary heard himself say, "Wait." He wasn't sure, afterward, what he'd intended beyond the word, but she turned, and now he had to have a plan.

"I live on your street," he said. "Four houses up. You returned our dog, the spring before last."

"Lucky," she said.

"If you're walking home anyway, I get my break in ten minutes. I could come by and take some off your hands." He heard it as he said it, how it sounded, and pressed on anyway. "You shouldn't have to carry a whole lasagna back."

Mr. Sow, from the table, said nothing at all, which Zachary chose to read as permission rather than its opposite.

The woman looked at him, then at the tray, then at the door. "You'd have to eat it at my kitchen table," she said. "I'm not giving you a plate to take into a yard."

"I can sit at a table," Zachary said.

Hilary had come over somewhere in this, still holding a bag of lentils. "You realize you've just solved a problem the food bank legally can't touch," she said, quietly, when the woman had gone out. "One hungry person at a time. By volunteering to be personally fed."

"It's not a system," Zachary said. "It's a lasagna."

"Everything's a lasagna until it scales," Yassine said, and went back to his sheet.

Zachary thought about it while he sorted, the small private transaction versus the shelf of dented cans, the woman's kitchen versus the warehouse of rules, and he could not make the two of them line up, and he suspected they were not supposed to. Mr. Sow ran a place that fed hundreds and turned away one tray; Zachary had fed, or would feed, one person, and would change nothing. It seemed to him that both of these were true and that being forced to choose between them was the actual job, and no one had put that on the laminated sheet.

At noon he took his gloves off. Yassine slapped his shoulder on the way out with a "polymath of the pantry, this one," which made no sense and was clearly meant as the highest compliment available. Hilary said she'd see him Monday, meaning she would ask how it went, meaning she would notice if he lied.

The woman's door was the one with the flag. He could smell the lasagna from the porch, and when she opened the door she was already carrying a fork.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
Maelie found her cousin at the folding table behind the incense stall, counting bills into a red envelope with the concentration of someone defusing something. The street festival had closed off three blocks of River Street: paper lanterns strung between the lamp posts, a stage where the lion dancers were waiting on their handlers, stalls of sesame balls and calligraphy scrolls and grilled squid whose smoke had already desiccated the air into something her throat noticed. Her cousin was eleven and had saved his money from birthdays and raking leaves.

Forty dollars. He had two twenties flat on the table and was folding them toward the envelope. The gift was for their grandmother, who had organized the festival's ancestor table for thirty-one years and had never once, as far as Maelie knew, been given anything by the grandchildren directly. He had decided this was the year to change that.

"Wait," Maelie said.

He looked up, annoyed, holding the bills the way you hold cards you don't want anyone to see. Behind them, a woman at the money-changing stall was handing out fresh red envelopes to whoever needed one, and taped to the front of her table was a hand-lettered sign listing auspicious amounts. Maelie read it while pretending to look at the squid stall. Thirty-eight. Fifty. Sixty-eight. A hundred and eight. Every amount on the sign avoided the number four, and every amount avoided it completely, in the tens place too. Forty was not on the list. She thought of her father once pulling a four-dollar bill out of a red envelope at New Year, laughing, saying it was like being handed a small funeral. She had been eight and had not understood, and no one had explained, and she had forgotten until right now.

"You can't do forty," she said.

"Why not? It's my money."

"Four sounds like death," Maelie said. "In the language. That's why the amounts on her sign are all those weird numbers."

He squinted at the sign, then at his twenties. "That's not real. That's just a coincidence."

Camelia appeared beside them with a cup of grass jelly and no warning, as she tended to. She went to their school, lived four streets over, and had opinions the way the festival had lanterns. "Whose superstition are we litigating?" she said, and Maelie explained the envelope, the forty, the grandmother. Camelia took a long sip and delivered her verdict. "Then the superstition is the externality here. You're not paying forty dollars, you're paying forty dollars plus an old woman's bad night. Cheap to avoid, honestly. Any rational person avoids it."

Maelie didn't answer, because the framing bothered her and she wanted to work out why before she said anything. Camelia's version made the avoidance a transaction, a tax on belief paid by nonbelievers to keep the peace. But her cousin's face had gone a different direction. He was now holding the two twenties like evidence at a trial. "If I change it, then I'm saying I believe it. And I don't. It's a number." He said it in the tone of someone testing whether it was true. Their father's whole generation treated the rule as background, done without thought; Camelia treated it as noise to be routed around; and their cousin, at eleven, was trying to decide whether a ritual could survive a person who didn't believe in it, or whether performing it anyway made him a liar.

The lion drum started somewhere near the stage, one deep beat, then a pattern. Their grandmother was by the ancestor table, straightening the fruit, adjusting the cups of wine that nobody drank. Maelie had watched her do it every year of her life. Whether the dead tasted anything, Maelie had no idea, and neither, she suspected, did her grandmother, who was also a woman who kept her receipts and questioned fortune cookies. She did it anyway. She had never once said why.

"Here's what I actually think," Maelie said. "You don't have to believe a number hurts someone to believe it communicates something. The envelope isn't about physics. It's about what the person opening it hears." She turned the forty dollars over in her mind. Keeping it said, I thought about the tradition and rejected it. Changing it said, I thought about you. Both were honest. She could not make the choice honest for him. "But I might be rationalizing, because I want it to be okay to do things I don't believe in. I don't fully know."

The eleven-year-old looked at the sign again, looked at the grandmother, and then did something Maelie hadn't predicted. He kept one twenty in the envelope and put the other twenty in his pocket, and at the money stall he traded it for a ten, a five, and five ones: thirty-eight dollars, the first amount on the sign, chosen so obviously, so deliberately, that Maelie knew he had made it a message on purpose. The avoidance of four ran so endemic through the whole festival, through the amounts and the table and the envelopes, that his small act of compliance didn't read as surrender. It read as joining.

He sealed the envelope and walked it over to the ancestor table, holding it out in both hands the way the fruit had been held earlier, during the offering. Their grandmother took it, looked at the sealed flap, then looked at him, and said nothing at all. She put it under the bowl of oranges where it would stay all evening.

"Thirty-eight," Camelia said, reading the sign upside down from where she stood. "So it's endemic, and you all just live inside it."

"He chose it," Maelie said.

The drum pattern broke into the fast section, and up the street the lion rose onto its hind legs, gold fabric rippling, close enough that they could see the sweat on the operator's wrists.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Linguist Merrill Swain's output hypothesis holds that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn.
story:
Sophie had chosen her grandmother's kitchen to practice because nobody there could correct her, and by the second evening she needed that mercy. The assignment was five minutes of unbroken argument, in French, on whether cities should ban private cars from their centers, and Ms. Wilson had made it worse by promising a live audience on Friday. Sophie spread her notes across the table where the oilcloth had faded into pale roses, and said her opening sentence to the window. "Les voitures privées devraient être interdites au centre-ville," she began, and then stopped, because she could not remember how to say "unless public transit improves first," and a five-minute argument that could not say "unless" was hardly an argument at all.

Kenneth had told her the trick on Monday, leaning across the lab bench while Ms. Wilson took attendance. "Don't write it out and memorize it," he said. "You'll sound like a vending machine. Just talk, and see where you fall down." She had thought this was lazy advice, the kind Kenneth gave so he could lionize his own improvisations later, but now, at the oilcloth table, she tried it. She talked. She fell down immediately. She wanted to say that correlation was not causality, that car-free streets in Paris might have reduced noise for other reasons too, and she could produce neither word. The gap opened under her like a missing stair.

Her grandmother was in the next room with the radio low, shelling peas into a chipped bowl. Sophie kept her voice at a mumble, but when she swore in English at the ceiling, her grandmother called out, "Encore?" without turning. Sophie said it was nothing, vocabulary. She tried again. She could say that cars polluted. She could say that people needed to travel. She could not connect the two ideas with anything stronger than "mais," and "mais" was doing the work of a whole bridge.

By Thursday she had pages of holes. She had discovered she couldn't say "congestion," couldn't say "air quality," couldn't phrase the conditional she actually believed in, which was that bans were justified only where transit existed already. It occurred to her, somewhere between the dictionary and the cold tea, that she had spent four years of French being praised for understanding everything and producing almost nothing, and that the praising and the silence had been the same problem. She found a phrase in her textbook's margins, an old note from a lecture Ms. Wilson had played them, something Swain had called the output hypothesis. Trying to speak, the note said, makes you notice the gaps in what you know, and noticing is what teaches you. Sophie read it three times. She had assumed her ignorance was a private inventory, something she could consult quietly and then display. Instead the gaps only appeared when she reached for them, in the reaching itself.

That was the thing she could say on Friday morning, though it wasn't germane to cars. Kenneth arrived after school to play opposing counsel, as they'd agreed, and they set the kitchen timer for five minutes and faced each other across the roses. Sophie began. Her French was slow and her grammar buckled, but she argued, and when Kenneth challenged her on Paris, she reached and found, to her astonishment, that she had learned "la corrélation" and "la causalité" during the night without deciding to. She said them out loud like new coins. He pushed back that freedom mattered more than clean air, and she pushed on the conditional, her real position, the one with "unless" in it, and it came out lopsided but whole.

At the four-minute mark, when Kenneth escalated, her grandmother rose from her chair, carried the pea bowl past them to the counter, and said, in accentless French, "Vous oubliez les livreurs, Sophie. The delivery drivers. Who speaks for them?"

Sophie stared at her. The timer ticked in its plastic way, and she had twenty seconds left of an argument that had just been folded open like a map. "Qui parle pour eux," her grandmother repeated, softer, and went back to her chair and her peas as though she had said nothing at all, as though forty years in this kitchen had not concealed a childhood in Lyon behind a mumbled radio and an uncorrected accent.

Sophie turned back to Kenneth, whose eyebrows had gone up so far they threatened his hairline. She took the thread. "Et," she said, "il y a une question que nous ignorons. Les livreurs." She built the last twenty seconds on the delivery drivers, on the people a ban helps and the people it quietly burdens, and the timer rang while she was still holding the sentence in the air, unfinished.

Later, on the porch, Kenneth asked the question under all the other questions. "Your grandmother. Did you know?"

Sophie looked through the window at the shelling, the steady thumbs, the radio murmuring in a language she had been performing all week while the person who owned it sat ten feet away. "No," she said. "Ask her about Lyon sometime."

"Will she answer?"

Sophie watched her grandmother tip the last peas into the pot. "Try me in French," the old woman called through the screen, and did not look up.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States.
story:
Hunter had spread the two books across his bed like opposing counsel. One was by a historian who argued that American anticommunism manufactured the Cold War, that a cautious Soviet Union had been encircled and provoked. The other, thinner and angrier, claimed Washington had fatally underestimated an expansionist oligarchy from the beginning. Mr. Bennett had assigned them side by side, then asked for a page weighing each against the evidence, and Hunter had spent two evenings discovering that weighing was harder than choosing.

Yasser arrived at seven with a bag of chips and no intention of helping. He settled into the desk chair anyway, spinning it in slow arcs, because Yasser's own essay was due Monday and his plan was to worry about it aloud in someone else's room rather than his own. "I'm just going to pick the one that's easier to argue," he said. "Bennett can't fail you for having an opinion."

"He can fail you for having an opinion the evidence doesn't support." Hunter turned the angrier book over and read the copyright page again, feeling something shift in his stomach. The author's first edition had come out in 1992. He picked up the other book, the anticommunism one, and checked its date: 1984. Neither man could have seen what Hunter was now reading about online, half-lit by the desk lamp.

"Listen to this," Hunter said. "The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages were released by the US government in 1995. They confirmed Soviet spy networks actually operated in the United States." He said it twice in his head. Both historians had written before the decrypts came out. Both had been arguing about espionage with half the documents missing, like jurors who never heard the recording.

Yasser stopped spinning. "So the second guy wins?"

"That's not how it works." Hunter pulled his notebook closer and began writing, the pen moving faster than his certainty. If the spy networks were real, then the anticommunist historian's core claim looked sturdier. But sturdier wasn't proven. One confirmed fact couldn't vindicate a whole turgid account of Soviet grand strategy, and it certainly couldn't excuse everything Washington had done in the name of vigilance. The first historian might have been wrong about espionage and right about paranoia, or right about both and wrong about causes, and Hunter had no way to sort which was which from a single page of decrypted cables. He wrote that down too: the question the evidence could not settle.

"There's a paragraph in the second one," Hunter said, flipping to it, "where he says the West had a duty to valorize its own principles, or something like that, and I thought it was fine when I read it. Now I'm not sure if he means defend them or worship them." Yasser shrugged, stole a chip, and said that Hunter was going to get a worse grade than people who just answered the question. But he pulled his chair closer to the bed and picked up the 1984 book, which surprised them both.

They worked for a while in a quiet that wasn't unfriendly. Hunter noticed that Yasser kept frowning at a passage about the Soviet system and finally said, almost to himself, "My grandfather used to say nobody in Moscow believed anything either." Yasser rarely mentioned his grandfather, and he didn't elaborate now; he just copied the page number into his phone and went back to spinning, slower.

When Yasser left, the hallway light went off and Hunter's mother called something about the hour from the kitchen, half question and half permission. Hunter stayed where he was, the two books still open, their arguments facing each other across the strip of blanket between them. He read his own last sentence, which said that the honest position was probably an uneven one, and crossed out the word "probably" because it felt like flinching. Then he wrote the new paragraph, and the pen was still moving when the house went quiet around him.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
The car sat in the driveway with its engine off and its passenger door already open, as if it had been waiting for him longer than he'd been ready to admit. Ms. Bautista, who had taught his cousin two summers ago and agreed to fit him in before September, set a clipboard on the dash and told him to adjust the mirror until he could see the edge of the garage door without moving his head. Jordan did it slowly. He had spent all spring telling people he didn't need a license yet, that Jackson drove them everywhere anyway, and all summer quietly regretting it, and now the regret and the wanting had collapsed into a single Saturday morning.

"Before we go anywhere," she said, "a question. If you double your speed, how much longer does it take to stop? Not a trick. Just guess."

He thought of physics class, of the graphs Mr. Whoever had drawn on the board while Jordan half-listened, and said, "Twice as long. Maybe a little more."

Ms. Bautista smiled the way a person smiles when they're about to be kind about being wrong. "Most people say that. It's about four times as long. Braking distance goes up with the square of your speed, so doubling the speed makes the stopping distance roughly four times what it was." She let that sit for a second, then said, "Buckle up."

He turned the key, backed out of the driveway with her hand hovering near the wheel, and they went around the block twice, then down to the empty parking lot behind the middle school. It was strange how quickly the pedals stopped feeling like accusations. By the third lap he could hold ten miles an hour without lurching, and he understood, in a small and private way, why Jackson drove like the road owed him something. Control was sweet. It could also desensitize you, he suspected, the way his cousin's laugh at eighty on the highway had stopped alarming anyone in the back seat, and he filed that suspicion somewhere behind the steering.

At the far end of the lot she had him stop at a chalk line she'd drawn, then drive to the other end and come back at what felt like walking speed. "Brake at the line," she said. He did, easily, the car settling a foot past it. Then she sent him back and told him to return at double that speed. He pressed the pedal the same way he had before, with the same confidence, and the car slid past the chalk and halfway to the fence before it stopped, and his hands were cold and his mouth was dry.

"That's the square," Ms. Bautista said, not unkindly. "You weren't careless. You just believed your foot instead of the math."

He sat with the wheel still in his hands. He thought of his father, who drove five over the limit always and called it prudent, and of the article Hilary had sent him last month about the city installing speed cameras downtown, which she'd captioned "finally, a technocracy that works" and which he'd argued with her about for a whole lunch period, insisting that machines deciding guilt felt worse than cops doing it, even when the machines were right. He had enjoyed the argument. He was less sure now, sitting in the marks his own tires had laid down, that rightness was a small thing to trade away just because it arrived without a face.

"Can we do it again?" he asked.

They did it four more times, and by the last one he was braking early, well before the chalk, and the car stopped short of the line with room to spare, and Ms. Bautista said, "Now you're being honest with the square."
