He laughed at that, and she laughed too, a short, saturnine chuckle that didn't quite match the softness of her eyes.

On the drive home he held twenty miles an hour on the residential street even when the road opened up and the car seemed to ask for more, and when a kid on a bike wobbled out of a driveway three houses ahead, he braked early and smooth and the car stopped with the whole width of a lawn to spare. The kid never looked up.

Back in his own driveway, engine off, he texted Hilary: you were more right than I said about the cameras. Then, before she could answer, he took the key out of the ignition and set it in Ms. Bautista's open palm. "Same time next week?"

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Seder plate holds maror, bitter herbs such as horseradish, which are eaten to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.
story:
The social hall of Temple Beth Am smelled of roasted eggs and vinegar, and Sienna stood at the head of the longest table she had ever been allowed to lead from. For eleven years she had watched her grandmother run the Seder from a folding chair at the front, tapping the table for silence, deciding when the candles were lit and when the youngest child sang the Four Questions. This year her grandmother was in a rehab facility in Clearwater, and she had handed the Haggadah to Sienna the way you hand someone keys, without ceremony, with the assumption that the car would be driven.

She had spent three weeks preparing. She had copied out the order of the service on index cards, color-coded them, then abandoned the cards when they made the whole thing feel like a biology exam. Her father had offered to requisition extra chairs from the synagogue office, a word he used for everything from furniture to attention, and by six o'clock there were thirty-one people seated, including Jaylynn, who had never been to a Seder in her life and had come because Sienna had said, "You can just come and eat, you don't have to know anything."

The trouble arrived with the maror. Sienna had grated the horseradish root herself that afternoon, crying over the bowl in her mother's kitchen, and it sat on the Seder plate now in its small heap beside the charoset, sharp enough that people two seats away were blinking. When the moment came, she explained the steps, and everyone took their bitter herb and their haroset and made the Hillel sandwich, and then she looked up and saw Jaylynn holding her piece of horseradish like it was evidence of a crime.

"Is this a mistake?" Jaylynn whispered across the table. "Like, did someone grate the wrong vegetable?"

"No," Sienna said, and then, because the whole table had gone quiet to listen to her, she kept going. "It's maror. It's on the Seder plate on purpose. They're bitter herbs, like horseradish, and we eat them to remember the bitterness of slavery in Egypt." She heard her own voice wobble and steadied it. "We're supposed to taste it. That's the point."

Jaylynn ate hers, went red, drank half a glass of water, and said, "Okay, that is genuinely awful," and Sienna's uncle, who could turn a discussion about parking into something bellicose, laughed harder than anyone and said, "That's my girl, she grates it stronger than Grandma ever did."

That should have been the easy part. The hard part came later, at the Four Children, where the Haggadah describes the wise child, the contrary child, the simple child, and the child who does not know how to ask. Sienna's grandmother always skipped the commentary and read straight through, brisk and unbothered. But Hamza, who had come with his Israeli lit teacher and was sitting near the far end, raised his hand like they were still in Ms. Baptiste's English class, and said, "So which one are you supposed to be? Is it good to be the wise child, or is that being smug?"

Sienna opened her mouth to give the answer she'd rehearsed, the one from the rabbi's Purim lecture about how every person contains all four children. It sounded, suddenly, like something borrowed. She thought about her grandmother, who read the text flat and let it mean what it meant, and about Ms. Baptiste, who spent whole classes on interpretation, who had once written the word hermeneutics on the board and said, "The text doesn't change; you do, and so does what you find in it." Two ways of holding the same book. Her grandmother would say the question was needless. Hamza was asking because the question mattered to him.

"I think you're allowed to be all of them," Sienna said. "Tonight I'm the one who doesn't know how to ask, honestly. I've done this my whole life and I've never once asked why we argue with the text instead of just reading it." She turned a page she had read a hundred times. "Maybe you're supposed to notice which child you are each year, and it's not the same every time."

Hamza considered this, nodding slowly, and her uncle muttered something about midnight and the afikoman, and the table moved on to dinner. But through the soup and the brisket, Sienna kept thinking about it, turning the two approaches over the way you turn a stone in your hand. She didn't have it settled. She knew only that she didn't want to inherit the Seder whole and unexamined, and she also didn't want to take it apart so thoroughly that nothing was left to hand on.

Near the end of the night, after Elijah's cup and the last verse of Chad Gadya, Jaylynn helped her carry the Seder plate to the synagogue kitchen. The maror was nearly gone, one shred of horseradish left on the white china.

"Do you save the plate for next year?" Jaylynn asked, running water into the serving bowls.

"We wash it and start over," Sienna said. She picked up the last shred of maror, held it a second, and ate it before she could think better of it. Her eyes watered instantly, and she laughed through it, and said, "Okay. That one was on me."

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: The Higgs boson discovery on July 4, 2012 was announced only after two separate CERN detector teams, ATLAS and CMS, independently found the same new particle.
story:
Abigail had measured the pendulum's period eleven times before she believed it, and even then she only half believed it, because the other half of her was already drafting the email she would send to Mr. Kim claiming that her value for g was right and the textbook's was wrong. She had checked the calibration twice, she told herself, and she had not rounded anything, and the number kept coming out at 9.64 rather than 9.81. Jaxen, working two benches over, kept glancing at her notebook in that way he had, sardonic and unhurried, as if he already knew how the period would end.

Mr. Kim's classroom still smelled of the glue from the poster he had put up in September, a photograph of a cavernous underground hall crisscrossed with scaffolding and cables. He had never said what it was. Abigail had assumed for most of the term that it was a cathedral, which, her grandfather would have told her, was not entirely wrong.

Her grandfather had taken her to the particle physics exhibit the summer she turned twelve, the last summer he could walk that far. She remembered a man at the display case, a stranger with a lanyard, asking why on earth they had built two enormous machines instead of one, whether it was waste or vanity. Her grandfather had read the plaque aloud in his patient, careful voice, the voice he used for anything he suspected was important. It said the discovery of the Higgs boson on July 4, 2012 had been announced only after two separate teams, called ATLAS and CMS, independently found the same new particle. "Two eyes," her grandfather had said afterward, tapping his cane on the floor. "One eye lies to you sometimes." She had been bored, she remembered, and had asked for ice cream, and he had acceded, as he almost always did.

In the classroom, on the Thursday, Mr. Kim collected everyone's values for g on the board without comment. Most of them clustered near 9.8. Hers did not. Neither did Jaxen's, which sat at 9.63, and Michael's partner's, which sat at 9.60, and one from a group near the window that Abigail didn't know well. Four groups out of nine, all low.

"Interesting," was all Mr. Kim said, which from him was practically a shout.

Abigail raised her hand and said that when four groups independently measured the same low value, that was evidence of a real effect, and that the class should not simply average toward the textbook. She said it well. She had practised the sentence on the bus. Jaxen looked at her for a long moment and then said, quietly, "We all used the same timers from the same box."

She wanted to argue with him. She wanted to say that independent measurements were independent, whatever the equipment, and she almost cited the poster at the back of the room, the two detectors, the date she still remembered for reasons she couldn't explain, July 4, 2012, two teams finding the same thing. But Jaxen was already walking to the cabinet, taking out the box of timers, and testing one against the wall clock, and then another, and the words stopped in her throat.

One timer ran slow. Then a second. By the end of the period he had checked all twelve, and three of them were slow by almost exactly the amount that would drag a pendulum measurement down to 9.64, and the three groups with low values had all drawn their timers from that box. Abigail had checked her calibration twice, she had told herself that morning, but when she actually thought back, honestly, she had checked it once, and briefly, because she had been so eager to have found something.

She stayed after the bell to redo the measurement with Michael's timer, and the value came back at 9.79, ordinary and correct. Michael leaned against the bench watching her. "You're not going to send that email to Mr. Kim, then," he said. It wasn't unkind. She shook her head and began coiling the string around her fingers.

Her grandfather would have liked Jaxen, she thought, watching him at the cabinet, methodical and unimpressed, no pedagogue about it, just a boy checking a clock against a clock. She had wanted so badly to be the one eye that saw truly, and instead she had been the one eye that lied, or that wanted to, which amounted to the same thing. Still, when she looked at the board with its four stubborn low numbers and its five obedient high ones, she felt something she couldn't quite call regret. The low numbers had meant something. They had meant the timers were broken, a finding nobody would have made if she had quietly deleted her outlier and moved on.

Mr. Kim erased the board slowly, wiping away the false gravity, and wrote in the corner, in his small even hand: check the instrument before you trust the world, or trust the world before you trust the instrument. He underlined neither. Abigail copied it into her notebook, then crossed out the second half, then crossed out the crossing out. Jaxen snapped the timer box shut and said, "Same lab again next year. New timers, maybe."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
The milking parlour smelled of iodine and warm animal breath, and Joshua had spread his biology notes across a feed bin because it was the only flat surface on his uncle's farm not covered in something living. Exam was Thursday. He was supposed to be helping with the evening chores, but the heifers were slow coming through the gate, and Mr. Korhonen, who rented the north field and still came round at dusk to look at the sky, had settled onto an upturned bucket beside him without asking what the papers were.

Joshua's problem was simple and enormous: he could not hold the whole process in his head at once. DNA unzipped, letters got copied into a message, the message got read, a protein came out the other end. He knew the words. He could recite them the way he could recite the Lord's Prayer without once thinking about God. Thursday would ask him to explain it, actually explain it, and reciting would not be enough.

"Read it to me," Mr. Korhonen said. "I got no idea what any of it means. That's why you should read it to me."

"You'll fall asleep."

"I fell asleep in church once and your aunt still brings it up. Read."

So Joshua read, stumbling, and the old man listened with his chin in his hand, and when Joshua got to the part about the message being read in groups of three, Mr. Korhonen stopped him. "Groups of three. Like counting seed in a row." He picked up a handful of cracked corn from the sack by the wall and laid kernels on the feed bin, three, three, three. "Go on."

Joshua laid down three corn kernels, then three more, and found himself whispering the letters, and the whisper turned into counting, and the counting turned into a question he had skipped past in the textbook because it was printed small. Four different letters, read three at a time. He did the arithmetic on the back of his hand with a pencil stub. Sixty-four. Sixty-four possible groups.

The heifers chose that moment to stampede through the gate, and Joshua's kernels went everywhere, and by the time the last cow was locked in a stanchion, the old man had gone home and Joshua had forgotten his own arithmetic. He found it again at the kitchen table, after washing his hands twice, while his uncle ate bread and honey and didn't ask about the exam because there was a kind of apportionment in the house, unspoken, of what got asked about and what got let alone. His father's hospital bills lived in that unasked half, and so, mostly, did Joshua's future.

Kelton texted a photo from the science museum two counties over, where his mother had dragged him for his little sister's birthday: a big wall chart, codons down the side, amino acids across the top. YOU SAID 64. THERE'S ONLY 20 THINGS ON THIS CHART, he wrote, followed by three question marks. Joshua sat very still with the phone in his hand. Twenty. He counted the chart's list twice from the blurry photo. Twenty amino acids, and sixty-four ways to write them, which meant, and he checked it against his own pencil arithmetic, that most of the amino acids had more than one group of three standing for them. The code was not a lock with one key. It was a language with synonyms, more words than meanings. He texted back nothing for a long minute, then: I HAD IT WRONG. YOU FOUND IT. He felt something he couldn't dichotomize into either gratitude or humiliation, so he let it stay whole and unnamed.

Ernest found him in the barn loft the next morning, where Joshua had gone to be alone with the chart and a printed copy of the museum photo. Ernest wanted to drive to the lake; Joshua said Thursday was coming; Ernest climbed the ladder anyway and sat against the hay bales with his sunglasses pushed up in his hair, performing an ascetic patience he did not actually possess, which they both knew, which was why it was funny.

"Explain it then," Ernest said. "For real. If you can explain it to me, you're fine."

Joshua started with the corn, because the corn had worked once already. He laid kernels in threes along the loft boards, one row for the message. Then he used pebbles for the sixty-four possibilities and only twenty bottle caps, and made Ernest watch while several pebbles crowded against a single cap, and Ernest said, "So it's saying the same thing different ways," and Joshua said "Redundancy," and Ernest said, "So it's your aunt saying supper's ready in four different voices," and that was the moment Joshua understood it completely, sitting in a dusty loft while his friend compared the fundamental machinery of life to his aunt, and he laughed harder than he had in months, aware even as he laughed that this was the last week anyone would be in this loft with him, that Ernest was leaving for a school out west and the farm would go on being the farm without either of them.

On Thursday he wrote for an hour and a half, and the question about the numbers came and he wrote sixty-four, twenty, most of them more than one, and did not add why, because he did not fully know why, and something in him respected that. Walking out past the gymnasium doors he found Kelton waiting, holding out his phone with the museum chart still on it.

"Still only twenty," Kelton said. "Checked it twice."

"Still sixty-four ways to say them," Joshua said, and took the phone, and held it a moment before giving it back.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
Maxime had agreed to volunteer mostly because Arianna said the warehouse was next to Maplewood, the seniors' residence where her grandmother lived, and he liked the idea of being the kind of person who showed up somewhere without being asked twice. He told himself, on the bus, that he would be good at this. He was organized. He could lift things. Besides, he had already imagined the whole morning: families arriving at the loading bay, grateful, and him handing over bags of rice with a modest, capable expression.

The warehouse was colder than he expected and much quieter. He found Arianna and Adrian stacking canned tomatoes onto pallets, and a supervisor who handed him a clipboard and told him to log incoming cases of pasta. Nobody arrived. He waited for the doorbell, the line at the counter, the whole scene he had rehearsed. By eleven he had logged two hundred cans of chickpeas and not one person had come for groceries, and he began to suspect, quietly, that he had misunderstood something basic about where he was.

"Where do all the people go?" he finally asked Arianna, gesturing at the shelves. "It's a food bank. Isn't the point that people come here?"

Arianna laughed, not unkindly, and Adrian looked up from his pallet with an expression Maxime chose to read as respect rather than pity. "The food bank is the warehouse," she said. "It collects everything and distributes it out to the local agencies. A food pantry is where people actually pick up the food directly."

"So nobody ever comes here."

"That's not the job," she said, and went back to her tomatoes.

He absorbed this the way one absorbs a failed prediction, and he would not have admitted, afterward, how much of his morning had been built on the version where he stood at the center of things. Instead he turned the clipboard over and wrote, on the back, a small diagram: warehouse in the middle, arrows going out to pantries,churches,schools. It was, he conceded, actually a more interesting design. Centralized collection, distributed access. Something about it pleased him, the way a good proof pleases him, though it also meant that the person who needed the food and the person who sorted it never had to meet, which seemed both efficient and slightly lonely.

At lunch the supervisor said they could eat on the terrace of Maplewood, since the residence shared a courtyard with the warehouse, and that a few residents liked to see young faces. This was how Maxime met Mr. Hosseini, who sat by a window with a thermos and who, when Maxime expostulated that the whole food bank system ran through a warehouse most people never saw, only shrugged and said, "Everything important is like that. The pipe is not the water."

Maxime wasn't sure he agreed. He sat with him anyway, and with Arianna's grandmother, who was telling Adrian about the year the whole courtyard garden died and came back different, and Maxime thought about how the woman's afternoon meals came from a pantry three streets away, stocked by the very warehouse he had been resenting all morning for its emptiness. He had wanted to hand someone a bag of rice. What he had done instead was move chickpeas along a chain he couldn't see the end of. Mr. Hosseini called the gap between one sort of work and another kind of result an interregnum, which Maxime thought was the wrong word, since there was no king involved, but he didn't argue, mostly because arguing with a man holding a thermos felt like a losing proposition.

What he did argue about, later, was the tomatoes. The supervisor wanted the dented cans separated for the agencies, and Arianna said her grandmother's pantry would still take them, and Maxime, feeling newly expert, said the warehouse rules were the warehouse rules. Arianna looked at him for a long second and said, "You've been here five hours." He stacked the dented cans in their own crate, sorted but not thrown out, which was less a compromise than a way of standing in two places at once, and he noticed that this was becoming his method for everything.

When he left, the light over the loading bay was the flat gold that makes October afternoons feel evanescent, already ending as they begin, and he stopped at the edge of the courtyard. Through the window Mr. Hosseini was still sitting with his thermos, and through the doorway behind Maxime the pallets stood ready for a truck that would come in the morning, and neither of them, the man or the truck, had needed him to understand anything.

"I'll be back Thursday," he told Arianna.

She hoisted her backpack. "Thursday we do the pasta."

"Thursday," he said, "I do the pasta," and pushed open the gate.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When entering a highway, drivers use the acceleration lane to reach a speed close to that of highway traffic before merging, since merging slowly forces others to brake.
story:
The cones in the church lot behind Grandpa's house had been set at what the handbook called "standard distance," though Grandpa had paced it off himself, his wedding ring clicking against the tape measure. Michael had been parallel parking between them for three days, and the third day was going worse than the first. He kept correcting, easing back, turning the wheel a degree at a time, and each correction bought him a smaller margin than the last.

"You're steering like you're apologizing," Grandpa said from the passenger seat, his cane braced against the floor mat. "Either commit or get out and walk."

Michael pulled forward and started again. This time he turned the wheel once, fully, and let the car rotate until the right mirror filled with cone. He straightened, crept backward, and stopped. When he got out and looked, the car sat inside the space with a hand's width at each end. It looked almost accidental, like the car had always belonged there.

"So it's not gentleness," Michael said. "It's decision."

"It's a lot of things," Grandpa said, which was his way of refusing to make anything simple.

That afternoon they drove to the highway. Grandpa needed his cardiology appointment across town, and Michael needed the merge, the one manoeuvre the test required and the lot couldn't teach. Daniella had texted him that morning: merge slow, safety first, her instructor had drilled it into her. It sounded right. It sounded like the kind of thing Michael believed about himself, that caution was the same as care.

The on-ramp climbed in a long curve, and Michael held the car at fifty while the traffic on the highway ran past on his left, close and continuous, a wall of moving metal. His foot hovered over the brake. Somewhere in him two ideas pulled against each other: the version of himself that slowed down when afraid, and the version that had turned the wheel once, fully, between the cones.

"Get up to their speed," Grandpa said, not raising his voice. "This is the acceleration lane. You match them before you go."

Michael pressed the pedal. The engine note climbed, the ramp straightened, and suddenly the wall of traffic wasn't a wall; it was cars going roughly his speed, one of them a blue hatchback with a gap in front of it that had opened as if by synchronicity, though Michael knew it was just a driver doing what drivers do. He slid into the gap. Nobody braked. Nobody honked. The merge was over before he had finished being afraid of it.

"That's it," Grandpa said, and looked out the window as if nothing had happened.

Driving home in the early light, Michael turned it over. Daniella's rule and Grandpa's rule weren't opposites, exactly, but they couldn't both be followed at once. Slowing into the merge would have forced the blue hatchback to brake; that was the whole trouble with it, that caution could be the danger. And yet he didn't want to conclude that boldness was simply the answer, that the cone lot had handed him a philosophy. Saying speed equals safety was nearly tautological if you only counted the times it worked. He thought of his mother, who had slowed at a yellow light last spring and been rear-ended anyway; he thought of Daniella's instructor, who presumably had reasons. What he actually knew was narrower and harder to hold: on this ramp, in this car, at this moment, accelerating had been the safer choice, and the proof was behind him in the traffic flowing unbroken.

The radio captivated Grandpa more than the drive did; he hummed along to a station that played big band, tapping one finger on his knee, and Michael realized his grandfather had stopped watching the road somewhere around the second mile. Not from trust exactly. More like fatigue, or the particular peace of a man who had decided this errand was worth the risk of it.

They turned back onto the county road, and Grandpa pointed at the lot with the cones, still standing in their patient line. "Pull in," he said. "Once more."

Michael parked between them in a single unbroken motion, and when he looked over, Grandpa was already asleep against the window, his cane sliding slowly sideways across the seat.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980 and fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases.
story:
Matthew had the graph taped above his desk like a wanted poster: a thin blue line crawling up through the 1970s, spiking, and then falling off a cliff. The assignment was to explain the cliff. Lincoln was coming over at seven to collate their notes into one presentation, and Matthew still could not say, out loud, why the line had fallen.

He had the numbers memorized. Inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980, and by 1983 it was below 3 percent. Between those two points the Federal Reserve had raised interest rates sharply. Somewhere in that gap was the answer, and he kept circling it the way you circle a word you can almost spell. He understood that higher rates made borrowing expensive, and that expensive borrowing made people spend less, and that less spending ought to calm prices. He understood each link alone. Strung together, they went slack.

Lincoln arrived with his laptop under his arm and a bag of sour candies, and he had his own agenda, which he announced while unwrapping the desk chair: he wanted the presentation to be funny. "Every econ presentation is a funeral," he said. "Ours should at least have a pulse."

"It has to be correct first," Matthew said.

"Correct and funny are not opposites." Lincoln dropped into the chair and spun once. "Ms. Hosseini said she grades on clarity. Clarity. I can do clarity with jokes."

They spread their notes across the bed. Lincoln had gathered cartoons, a clip of a man burning money for heat in 1979, a joke about mortgage rates so high that banks apologized. Matthew had the graph and a page of sentences he'd written and crossed out. He read one aloud, the cleanest one: "When the central bank raises rates, borrowing costs more, so people and businesses borrow and spend less, and slower spending eases pressure on prices."

Lincoln tilted his head. "Okay, say it like you're telling my mom why her savings account suddenly matters."

Matthew tried. "It's like the whole economy is an archipelago, and cheap loans are bridges between the islands. When rates go up, the bridges get tolls. Fewer people cross. The islands quiet down."

Lincoln pointed the candy at him. "That one. That one, right there. Use that one." He typed it into the slide, then frowned at his own screen. "But wait, the toll thing, is that actually why it dropped then? In the eighties?"

That was the question Matthew had been circling all week. He pulled up the graph again and put his finger on the peak. "Inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980," he said. "Below 3 percent by 1983. After the Fed raised rates sharply. That's the fact we have to hang the whole thing on."

"So it worked," Lincoln said.

"It worked here. In those years. I keep wanting to say it always works, and I can't prove that from one cliff." Matthew tapped the page of crossed-out sentences. "My dad says the rates back then also put people out of work, that it wasn't free. He remembers his uncle's loan office going under."

Lincoln leaned back. "So we say it worked and it cost something."

"Can we say both? Ms. Hosseini keeps asking us for a considered position, not a slogan."

From the hallway, Ms. Hosseini would not have heard any of this, and in fact she heard none of it; she was three houses down, in her own kitchen, unaware that two of her students were arguing about her rubric. What she had said in class, days earlier, was only that graphs were arguments, and Matthew kept returning to the phrase the way you return your tongue to a loose tooth.

They rebuilt the slides. Lincoln kept one cartoon and gave up the burning money, and in exchange Matthew let him title the cliff slide "The Drop." They wrote the toll bridge paragraph, then the numbers, then a final slide with a single line: rates went up sharply, inflation fell steeply, and what it cost was a question they were leaving open. Lincoln read it aloud twice. "It's honest," he said. "Is honest allowed?"

"It has to be," Matthew said. "Otherwise we're just decorating the graph."

Lincoln packed his laptop, left three candies on the desk as payment, and paused at the door with his hand on the frame. "One more run-through tomorrow at lunch?"

Matthew nodded, already looking back up at the taped line, at the peak and the long fall after it, tracing the drop with one finger.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
Aiden arrived at the community garden at eight, ten minutes early, which he regretted immediately because it gave him time to see the line. It stretched from the greenhouse door, past the raspberry canes, and along the chain-link fence almost to the bus shelter. On a Tuesday. He had assumed weekends were the busy days, when people were off work, and a weekday would mean folding tables and quiet arithmetic.

"You're the new one," said a woman in a canvas apron, handing him a clipboard. Ms. Farah, according to the email thread. "Garden side today. Cut kale, bundle it, bring it to the wash station. The food bank shares this site, so everything you harvest goes out that door within the hour."

He worked between two older women he didn't get names from, snapping stems and laying the bundles on damp newspaper. Through the greenhouse glass he could see the line advancing in small shuffles, a man reading a paperback, a girl about his sister's age with earbuds in, a teenager he half recognized from school. Jules. From grade eleven chemistry. Jules was standing in the food bank line with a folded duffel bag under his arm, and Aiden ducked back toward the raspberry canes before deciding whether that counted as hiding.

At the wash station he found Naomi, who had signed them both up for this, ostensibly for the volunteer hours their school required and actually, Aiden suspected, for reasons she hadn't stated.

"Long line for a Tuesday," he said.

"That's normal now." She turned a bundle of kale under the tap. "Food Banks Canada does a count every year. The new one, HungerCount 2025, recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. A record for a single month."

"March," Aiden said. "One month."

"One month." She shook water off the stems. "My mom quotes it at city council meetings. She's a pragmatist about it, she says, which mostly means she thinks saying the number out loud is a strategy. Some people at those meetings want to excoriate the councillors instead, and she thinks that feels good and fixes nothing. They fight about it in the parking lot afterwards."

Aiden carried the kale to the greenhouse door, where the boxes were going out. The man with the paperback took a box and thanked him by name, which was strange until Aiden saw he was reading the volunteer badge clipped to his own shirt. The girl with earbuds took a box almost as tall as she was, and Aiden watched her balance it on one hip and hold the door with her elbow, and nobody helped her, and she didn't look like she wanted anyone to.

He went back to the garden rows and cut kale without thinking about kale. He had come here with a theory, though he hadn't called it that, even to himself: that volunteering was an ascetic sort of act, doing something unglamorous for no reward, and that the reward was precisely the unglamorousness, the proof of it, the line on a form. Ms. Farah had a different theory, he could tell, one where the harvest mattered and the feelings of the harvester were beside the point, and Naomi's mother had a third, about numbers spoken into microphones. All three theories ended at the same greenhouse door with the same boxes, and Aiden could not figure out whether that meant they were the same theory or that theories were a luxury the line didn't have time for.

Jules was four people from the front now. Aiden made a decision and unmade it twice, then walked over with a bundle of kale he wasn't supposed to be holding.

"Hey," he said.

"Aiden, right? Sodium lab." Jules looked at the kale, then at the line ahead of him, then at the ground. "My uncle's place fell through, so we're at my aunt's, and there's eleven of us, so. It's this or my aunt skips meals so the little kids don't, and she'll do it, she's done it before, so it's this."

"You don't have to explain it."

"You looked like you were going to ask."

"I wasn't." It came out sharper than he meant, and then, because Jules was still looking at him: "Chem marks. My mom's on my case about chem marks and I'm out here for a form signature. That's the whole story."

Jules almost smiled. "Ascetic, man. Very monastic."

"I don't think that word means a school form."

"Close enough." The line moved and Jules moved with it, duffel bag under his arm, and at the table he took a box and put the kale Aiden had given him on top of it, deliberately, like a signature on something.

Aiden went back to the rows. The two older women had moved on to chard. He picked up his shears and worked beside them, and when he carried the next crate to the greenhouse, Ms. Farah met him at the door and looked at the empty space where the line had been, all the way to the bus shelter, and said, "Same again Thursday. You'll come?"

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
story:
Brayden had told his mother, twice, that stoichiometry was the easiest unit in chemistry, and by the third time he said it he half believed it, which was as good as believing it. He walked into Mr. Torres's lab fourth period carrying his notebook like a completed argument. The setup on the board was the one they'd drilled all week: given a mass of reactant, calculate the moles of product, using molar mass as the bridge. Five grams of sodium bicarbonate reacting with vinegar, producing carbon dioxide. Divide by molar mass, follow the coefficients, convert. He'd done it at his desk the night before, headphones on, in eleven minutes, and he'd written the answer in ink, which was how certain he was.

Ismail arrived carrying a cardboard box, which was typical. Ismail treated every lesson like something you could hold. He set it on the bench beside their shared station and Brayden measured it with his eyes and decided it was nothing, a prop, the kind of thing Ismail did instead of getting the numbers right.

"Twenty-two point four litres," Ismail said, rapping a knuckle on the side. "I measured it last night with a tape measure and cut it myself. One mole of an ideal gas takes up about twenty-two point four litres at zero degrees Celsius and one atmosphere." He said it plainly, the way he said everything, and Brayden felt a small irritation, because the fact was beautiful and Ismail had found it first.

The lab went ahead. Mr. Torres drifted between benches with his coffee, saying almost nothing, which Brayden interpreted as respect for students who didn't need help. The baking soda went into the flask, the vinegar followed, the fizz climbed the glass, and the tubing carried the gas into an inverted bottle in the water trough. Brayden wrote his numbers in the margin: five grams divided by eighty-four grams per mole, roughly point oh six moles of bicarbonate, and one mole of gas for every mole of it, and point oh six times twenty-two thousand four hundred because litres meant cubic centimetres, obviously, everyone knew that. He wrote one thousand three hundred litres. Then, feeling generous with his own brilliance, he crossed it out and wrote one hundred and thirty-four. He looked at the box. He looked at his page. The page said the gas from five grams should fill that box about six times over, should fill the room's corner, should be visible from the street.

The bottle in the trough filled, tipped, and stopped. Brayden bent to read the water line. He read it again. The gas occupied something like a litre and a third, a swallow of space, quiescent at the surface of the water as if it had never intended to be more.

He did not say anything for a while. Van leaned over from the next station, squinting at the bottle, then at Ismail's box, then at Brayden's margin. "Your answer says the ceiling should be gone," Van said. "The ceiling's fine."

Brayden turned back a page in his notebook, and here was the part he had not told his mother: the homework he'd finished in eleven minutes was finished because he'd copied the setup from a photo Ismail had sent when Brayden said he was stuck, and he had copied it without checking the units, and he had told himself, at the time, that checking was a formality for people less quick than he was. He sat with that. The room hummed with other people's reactions, other bubbles, and Mr. Torres was by the window now, watching the parking lot as though the class were something he had set in motion and could leave alone.

"There's twenty-two point four litres in one mole," Brayden said slowly, and saying it aloud he heard where he'd gone wrong, the way you hear a wrong note only after the phrase is over. "I multiplied by twenty-two thousand four hundred. Like it was centimetres. It's just twenty-two point four litres. The number's the number." He ran it again on a clean line: point oh six moles times twenty-two point four litres, about one point three litres. He looked at the bottle. The water line was exactly where the new arithmetic said it should be, and the old answer, the confident one, lay crossed out in the margin looking like what it was.

Ismail hadn't eulogized the box, hadn't given any speech about what it meant; he had just built it and set it there like an argument that didn't require a voice. Brayden thought of the philosophy YouTube channel he'd half watched last week, some video claiming existentialism meant the universe gives you no answers and you have to build your own, and he thought that chemistry was the opposite, or maybe not the opposite at all, because the answer was there but you still had to build your own way to it, and the building could go wrong, and nobody was going to tell you except the water line in a bottle. He wasn't sure which it was. He wrote the uncertainty in the margin, next to the crossed-out number, where he could find it again.

Mr. Torres came over at last and looked at the bottle, the box, the margin, in that order, and raised an eyebrow at the crossed-out figure. "So which one's the answer?" he asked.

Brayden picked up his pen, uncapped it, and drew a slow circle around one point three litres. "This one," he said. "But give me a second before you mark it."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Noemie had read the psychology chapter twice on the bus, which was one time more than necessary, and she knew that. The date was with a boy from her econ seminar who had asked her out in the middle of a sentence about supply curves, so quietly that she had made him repeat it. Joanie and Taryn had opinions. Joanie said arrive late, keep him guessing; Taryn said arrive early, help him relax. Noemie had preempted the whole argument by deciding to arrive exactly on time, which felt less like a decision and more like a refusal to have the argument at all.

The bowling alley smelled of rented shoes and Diet Coke, an atavistic smell, older than her, older than anyone in the building probably, the smell of every Friday night since the invention of teenagers. Mr. Wong, who owned the place and had coached her sixth-grade league, was restocking the concession shelf when she came in. He looked at her shoes, then at her face, and said, "Lane eight. He's already there. He got you the bumpers turned off, which I told him was a mistake."

He was on lane eight, and he was competent, which surprised her. He worked at the pharmacy, he'd told her once, and she watched him set his feet, swing, release, and knock down eight pins with a kind of modest efficiency. He picked up the spare. When his turn came again he did the same thing. She was bowling badly and did not mind, because his competence was interesting to watch, the way anyone's is when you're trying to decide what you think of them.

Then the cola happened. He reached for it mid-sentence, gesturing at something, and the cup went over, brown fizz spreading across the scoring table, pooling toward her phone, dripping off the edge onto his own shoe. He apologized four times in a row, and his face did the thing faces do when someone is certain the evening has ended before the second game. He got paper towels from the counter and knelt wiping the floor, saying, "I'm so sorry, that's it, that's the whole night ruined, you should just go."

Noemie did not go. Instead she heard herself say, "In 1966, this researcher, Elliot Aronson, and his colleagues ran an experiment. A highly competent quiz contestant spilled a cup of coffee, and afterward people rated him more likable. It's called the pratfall effect." The sentence came out too fast, the way facts do when you've been holding them. He looked up from the floor with the paper towels still in his hand.

She kept going, slower. She told him she'd read it that morning, and that she'd been turning it over all day, because there was something in it that bothered her. If she told him the spill made him more likable and she was only saying it to calm him down, then the kindness was a calculation, and if it was a calculation she hadn't really earned the moment, she'd manufactured it. And there was a second problem, worse, which was that the experiment was about strangers watching a contestant. She wasn't a stranger. She was supposed to be deciding whether she liked him, not applying a finding. "It feels like cheating," she said. "Like I'm grading you with someone else's rubric."

He stood up, wadded the towels, and threw them toward the bin, and missed, which they both noticed and neither mentioned. "So do you like me more now," he asked, "or is that a question the experiment can't answer?" She said she honestly didn't know, and that she thought the honest part might matter more than the liking part, though she couldn't prove that either, and there was no chapter to cite for it. He sat back down and typed his name into the scoreboard where the machine had erased it, and said, "Then we should probably bowl the second game, for data."

When her turn came she rolled the ball too hard and it hooked into the gutter, and she laughed at herself before he could, and he laughed too, not kindly exactly, but with her. Mr. Wong came by with a fresh cola, set it down well away from the table's edge, and said nothing at all.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
Faith had told Hanna the truth, mostly, which was that she liked Dev beyond all reasonable accounting, and that the movie started at seven, and that if she was standing alone under the marquee at six fifty-five she would die. The part she had left out was smaller, or she told herself it was smaller, and she had been practicing the leaving-out of it all week, the way you practice a speech until the words stop feeling like lies.

She arrived early anyway, because being early was a way of controlling something, and bought the tickets before he got there so she wouldn't have to stand at the register deciding whether reaching for her wallet counted as rude or as independent. The theater smelled like carpet shampoo and liquid butter. The horror preview poster in the lobby showed a swimmer in open ocean, tiny against something pelagic and half-glimpsed beneath her, and Faith stared at it until the water seemed to move.

"You're here," Dev said, arriving at 6:49, which she noted and then hated herself for noting. He had a way of standing with his hands in his pockets that suggested he was holding himself down. "Fair warning, I cover my eyes. My sister calls me a misanthrope but that's not even the right word. I like people. I just don't like whatever's in this movie."

"That's the opposite of a misanthrope," Faith said. "You're fine."

They took their seats in the middle row, not the back, because the back had a reputation and the middle had none. Her phone buzzed once in her pocket: Hanna, asking whether he'd shown. She didn't answer. Six minutes to previews, and she had a private deadline that no one had set but her: by the time the lights went all the way down, she would know, from the feeling in her own chest, whether she actually liked him or whether she'd invented him over the summer out of boredom and proximity.

The movie was louder than she expected. Somewhere in the first twenty minutes a door opened onscreen and something came out of it and her heart went off like a fire alarm, and Dev grabbed the armrest between them, and she grabbed it too, and for a moment their hands were stacked on the same plastic bar like two people reaching for the same ledge.

"Sorry," he whispered.

"It's fine," she whispered, and meant it, and then did not know if she meant it, because her heart was still pounding and she couldn't tell what it was pounding about.

She thought about something Mr. Littlechild had mentioned in psychology, half a sentence she'd caught while passing his door, about a study and a bridge, and afterward she'd looked it up on her phone in the library because she couldn't stand not knowing. In the dark now she reconstructed it: in 1974, Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron found that men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge. That was all she had. Same woman, two bridges. The scary bridge made the phone ring.

"Can I tell you something weird?" she said quietly, over the soundtrack of someone breathing in a closet onscreen.

"Obviously."

"In 1974, Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron did a study where men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge."

Dev turned his head. In the flickering light his expression was half lit and half gone. "So a scary bridge makes you think you like someone."

"I don't know if it's makes," Faith said, though honestly she didn't know what else to call it. "I just know that's what happened."

"So this movie," he said, and his hand was still on the armrest, close to hers, "is a bridge."

Which was exactly the problem she'd been circling for twenty minutes, laid out by a boy who covered his eyes at doors. If her heart was pounding, she couldn't read it. It might be him. It might be the movie. It might be him because of the movie, which was somehow the worst option, because then whatever she decided tonight would be built on a foundation she couldn't inspect.

The thing she hadn't told Hanna surfaced then, the way withheld things surface at the worst time: two weeks ago, when she'd first said Dev's name with feeling, Tessa had been sitting right there, and Tessa's face had done something Faith pretended not to see. Maybe she had liked him. Maybe Faith had wanted Tessa to know she could. The thought arrived without any evidence, which made it worse, not better, because a feeling that survives without evidence is usually the load-bearing kind.

The screen went quiet before the last scare, the sound draining out of the theater the way water drains from a tub, and everyone leaned forward. Faith looked down at the armrest, at the small dark space between his hand and hers, and felt her heart going, going, going, and understood that the study had given her a question and not an answer, and that the lights were nearly all the way down, and that a sturdy bridge and a frightening one both get you across.

She moved her hand one finger's width toward his and watched the screen, where the swimmer was alone now in all that open water, waiting to find out what was underneath her.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In NLRB v. J. Weingarten (1975), the US Supreme Court ruled that unionized workers may request a union representative at an interview they reasonably believe could lead to discipline.
story:
Sadie clocked in at four and found the schedule taped beside the time clock had changed again. Her Thursday shift, which had ended at nine for the past month, now ended at eleven, past the bus's last run, and the two hours had landed on a school night. She stood in the aisle with her backpack still on and read the sheet twice, as if the numbers might rearrange themselves.

"You got moved too?" Morgan came around the endcap with a armful of dented cans for the discount bin. Morgan worked the register and the dairy case, sometimes both in one shift, and had been at Fowler's Market for two years, longer than anyone else under twenty-five. "They did it to Tyce last week. Nobody asked. Nobody said anything."

Sadie had said nothing plenty of times herself. She needed the job for tuition money her parents couldn't cover, and she had learned fast that baggers who complained got the closing shifts and then fewer shifts until there were none. Still, eleven o'clock meant her mother driving across town at midnight, and it meant calculus homework done in the break room, which never went well. She did the math on the walk home and it came out like an asymptote, her savings creeping toward tuition and never quite reaching it, every extra hour closing a gap that stayed open.

The next afternoon Tyce found her in the cereal aisle. "They called Ms. Das into the office," he said. "Ricky from the kitchen. No, wait, Ms. Das is the union steward. They called her because they called Ricky in." Tyce tended to tell stories in the order the details occurred to him. "The manager wants to talk to him about the broken cooler log. Ricky signed it last Tuesday and it was wrong, and he thinks he might get written up, maybe fired. He's sweating. But Ms. Das came in with her cart of returns like it was nothing."

Sadie followed him to the front, where she could see the office door through the glass of the customer service counter. Ms. Das, who was sixty and had been at Fowler's since before the store was remodeled, stood in the doorway. "Ricky asked for her," Tyce said. "Did you know you can do that? If you're in the union and you're called into a meeting and you think it could lead to discipline, you can ask for a union representative to be there. It's your right. Court said so, supreme court, 1975." He said it the way he repeated things he'd heard, not entirely sure he had it right.

They watched Ms. Das go in and the door close. Sadie had assumed the union was mostly a line item on her paycheck, three dollars and some cents, which she'd privately resented. She had also assumed that the way things were was just the way things were, the way a floor is where it is. Now she was recalculating. The schedule, the hours, the cooler log, the office with the glass door: these were conditions, and conditions were things someone had set and someone could contest. She wasn't sure the union was purely altruistic, the way some of the older workers described it, a family, a shield. It was an organization, and it collected dues, and its steward shopped at this store like everyone else. Both things could be true.

When Ms. Das came out forty minutes later, she stopped at the service counter to sign the incident binder, and Sadie, restocking the candy there, heard her on the phone. "Written warning, no termination, and the schedule change is a separate grievance," Ms. Das said. "It's posted like it's a favor, but extended hours without notice is a change in working conditions, and we're filing." She hung up and looked at Sadie over the binder. "You're on Thursday until eleven, I hear."

"Yes," Sadie said. "Can I do anything about it? I'm not even full union yet, I think."

"You paid your initiation, you're a member, and members file grievances. There's a form in the break room." Ms. Das took her returns cart and rolled it toward produce. "Or don't. Plenty don't. But the ones who don't tend to keep closing."

At the end of her shift, before the new schedule took effect, Sadie sat in the break room with the grievance form in front of her and her calculus book unopened beside it. Morgan came in for a jacket and saw the form. "You're actually filling that out." Sadie thought about the tuition gap that never closed, about dues, about Ms. Das saying or don't, and picked up the pen anyway. She wrote her name in the first box and started on the second.

"Can I see it when you're done?" Morgan asked, pulling a stool over.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
The shrimp arrived first, arranged in a fan on cracked ice, and Evan's uncle lifted one and said, "So, tomorrow you walk." Across the table his grandmother was already crying, quietly, into her napkin, as though she had been saving the tears all week and could not hold them past the appetizer. The restaurant was the one his family used for every occasion that mattered, the room in the back with the lazy Susan and the boreal blue walls that his mother said were calming and his father said were cheap. Evan kept his phone face down beside his chopsticks.

He had written a valedictory speech, and at two o'clock that morning he had deleted it.

"So what do you say up there," his uncle pressed. "Something inspiring. Something they'll remember."

"Something short," Evan said, and everyone laughed, and Rian, sitting at his elbow, did not laugh.

Rian had read the speech. Lyna had read the speech too, in the library on Tuesday, both of them leaning over his laptop while he squirmed. It had ended with a quotation he had found at midnight, attributed in his head to Shakespeare, and it had sounded, in the fluorescent light, exactly like the kind of line a graduation deserved. Then at two in the morning, unable to sleep, he had looked it up to make sure. The line was Elgar. Or rather it was neither, exactly: Pomp and Circumstance was Elgar, the march everyone would sway to tomorrow in their gowns, and Elgar had taken the title from Othello, which mentioned the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war. The phrase Evan had lifted for his ending was Othello's, and he had filed it in his mind under music, under graduation, under the long green field in June, and never once under war.

"Speech is tomorrow," his father said, raising his glass. "Eleven a.m. We leave the house at nine sharp."

"Nine," Evan said. His mouth was dry. The lazy Susan turned, carrying the duck toward him, and he let it pass.

Lyna had arrived late, hair still damp from the shower, and had squeezed in beside his grandmother. Now she leaned across the plates and said, low, "You okay? You look like you're at a funeral."

"I'm fine."

"He's rehearsing," Rian said, and helped himself to rice.

He was not rehearsing. He was dismantling. The problem was not the quotation itself, which was honest enough if he said where it came from; the problem was everything he had built on it. The speech had been about arriving, about procession, about the swell of strings under the stadium lights, and now that music had a war in it, pride and glory walking in step, and he could not unknot the two. His grandfather, three seats down, was telling the story about carrying a rifle at eighteen that he told at every dinner, and no one at the table heard it the way Evan suddenly did, as a story about circumstance and about pomp, and he could not tell whether that made the story worse or more true.

The cake came out with a single sparkler in it. His family sang. His grandmother gripped his wrist and said, in their own language, that he was the first, the first of all of them, and he said yes, I know, and did not say what he was actually thinking, which was that the first is the one everyone watches when the music starts.

Outside, on the sidewalk, while the adults settled the bill and argued over who had paid last time, Lyna caught his sleeve. "It's the quote, isn't it. The one from your ending."

Evan looked at the restaurant window, at his family glowing inside it. "It's Shakespeare," he said. "But it's also Elgar. He named the march after it. Everyone thinks of caps and gowns, and it's actually about war." He heard how it sounded, like trivia, like a thing a connoisseur of footnotes would say at a party, and he added, "I don't know which one I'm walking to tomorrow."

"That's the whole thing though," Lyna said. "It can be both. People can be both."

"Can they?"

"You interpolated two things into your speech that were never together," Rian said, appearing beside them with toothpicks. "That's literally your English grade. Fix the ending, keep the middle."

Evan took out his phone. The blank document glowed. His father called from the doorway that it was time to go, that he needed sleep before the big day, and Evan stood under the streetlight typing one sentence, then deleting it, then typing it again. Lyna read over his shoulder.

"Read it out," she said.

"'We borrowed our music from a war,'" Evan said, "'and we are not marching anywhere except into the rest of our lives.'" He looked up. "Too much?"

Rian took the last toothpick and pointed it at the phone. "Send it to yourself," he said. "Before you change your mind again."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US National Labor Relations Act does not cover government employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, supervisors or independent contractors.
story:
Kyle clocked in at four, tied his apron, and counted the fry baskets that needed re-oiling before the dinner rush. On the schedule taped to the walk-in door, his hours for next week had been cut from thirty-eight to twenty-two, and beneath the schedule someone had written, in the chef's blunt pencil, "see me."

He had seen the chef already. The conversation had lasted under a minute. Business was slow, the chef said, and anyway Kyle was lucky to have a job at eighteen. When Kyle mentioned that Zayden, who worked the banquet kitchen at the hotel downtown, made four dollars an hour more for the same prep work, the chef laughed once, without warmth, and told him to stop denigrating the place that paid him. The word hung there, too big for the man using it, and Kyle went back to his onions.

Zayden's hotel kitchen was union. That was the whole of the difference, as far as Kyle could tell. Zayden got overtime past eight hours, got a break that actually happened, got a shop steward with a phone number taped inside his locker. On Friday, Kyle rode the bus downtown with Zayden to the union hall, a narrow brick building that smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, where a woman at the front desk handed him a stack of authorization cards and a folded sheet of paper. The sheet summarized the law, the National Labor Relations Act, the one that made the cards mean something.

Calder was with them, which Kyle regretted by the second paragraph. Calder had spent every summer since he was fourteen walking bean fields and detasseling corn for a crew boss who paid in cash and changed the rate whenever it rained. He read the paper with his lips moving slightly, then stopped and read one sentence again, silently, and his face changed. He held it out to Kyle. Kyle read it: the Act did not cover government employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, supervisors or independent contractors. He read it twice, because it seemed to drop a wall across the road they were all standing on.

"So it's not just me being lazy or complaining," Calder said. His voice was flat, which was worse than if he had yelled. "It's written down. Farm work doesn't count."

Kyle remembered, then, his mother's hands the winter the plastics plant closed. She had been a steward there once, or something like it; he'd been eight, and he remembered a meeting in their kitchen, her voice steady while a man from management talked in circles, each clause bending away from the last, until his mother finally said, "That's enough casuistry for one night." Kyle hadn't known the word. He'd looked it up later and kept it, the way you keep a stone that fits your palm.

At the restaurant, the organizing moved slower than Kyle wanted. Two dishwashers signed cards on the loading dock, and a server named nobody special said maybe, and then the chef found out. He called Kyle into the dry storage room between the flour sacks and the mop buckets, and stood close enough that Kyle could smell the garlic on his breath. "You file those cards," the chef said, "and I'll find a reason to let you go before the vote happens." His truculent certainty should have frightened Kyle, and it did, but underneath the fear something else moved, a kind of clarity, as if the room had fewer shadows than usual.

That was when Ms. Fitzgerald came in, the woman from table six who ordered the same trout every Thursday and tipped in exact change. She had worked, she said once, thirty years at the county hospital, and tonight she watched the chef loom by the pass and watched Kyle carry the trash out the back and said only, "You look like a man doing arithmetic."

He was. He sat on the milk crate behind the dumpster with the cards in his jacket, three signatures and room for more, and he thought about Calder, who couldn't sign anything like this no matter what, because the paper downtown had drawn its line and left him on the far side of it. Kyle could file. That much the law gave him. Whether filing would hold against a chef who lied about receipts and schedules, whether the others would stand up when it got expensive, whether Zayden's four extra dollars would ever cross the street to this kitchen, none of that was arithmetic he could finish tonight.

He took out his phone and texted Calder: you coming by after your shift. Then he squared the cards against his knee, folded them into his back pocket, and pushed through the door into the steam and the clang of the line, where the chef was already shouting for his onions.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
The portal refreshed at 3:47 in the afternoon, and Logan's status still read "Application Complete," which it had read for sixty-two days. He closed the laptop, walked to the kitchen, ate half an apple, and came back, because the alternative was sitting in his room doing nothing, and at least at the computer he was technically doing something.

He had applied to one school early, been deferred in December, and since then he had built a small ritual around the checking: portal first, then email, then the admissions blog, which updated on Tuesdays with posts like "A Day in the Life of Our Review Staff." He had read every one. This Tuesday's post was about the incoming class taking shape, and it used a word he had seen before but never stopped on: yield. The sentence said the admissions office was "monitoring yield projections carefully this cycle." Logan read it three times, then opened a chat window with Zack.

"what's yield," he typed, "in admissions talk."

Zack replied with a shrug emoji and "idk ask Gurman, he did the tour." Gurman had dragged Logan along to an open house in October, before any of this waiting started. Logan found the notes app on his phone where he'd written things down that day, mostly dining hall prices, and at the bottom a fragment he'd forgotten: guide said they're proud of their yield, asked him after. He called Gurman instead of texting, which felt drastic, but the waiting had made drastic things feel normal.

"It's the percentage of students they admit who actually accept and enroll," Gurman said, when Logan asked. "That's the whole thing. That's what yield is. The guide was bragging about it on the tour like it was a ranking." Gurman's mother said something in the background about the stove, and he said he had to go, but first he asked, "Why, did you get in?"

"No. Still nothing."

Logan sat with that for a second, the fact of it, the way a number could be a source of pride for a school and a source of dread for him. He opened a spreadsheet he'd been keeping, which his father called obsessive and which Logan privately thought of as research. On it he'd listed his schools in columns: acceptance rate, his GPA against the middle fifty percent, distance from home. He added a new column and typed the word yield at the top, though he only knew the number for one school, and that from a forum post of uncertain reliability.

What occurred to him, slowly, over the next hour, was that he had been thinking about admissions as something happening to him, a verdict being prepared in some subterranean office where his file sat in a folder with a sticker on it, and that this was only half true. The school had its own waiting to do. It would admit a batch of students in March and then spend April not knowing how many would say yes, and its yield, the percentage who accepted, would determine things he had never thought about: dorm space, section sizes, whether the freshman seminar he wanted would exist at all. He was applying to them and they were, in a strange mirrored way, applying to him, or at least to a projected version of him, some number in a model. He didn't find this comforting exactly. He found it clarifying, the way finding out a magic trick is done is clarifying: you still don't have the trick, but you know what kind of thing it is.

His mother came home at six with groceries and found him still at the desk, three browser windows open. He tried to explain, and it came out badly, something about how they need us too, and she set down the bags and said, "So what does that mean for you?"

"I don't know yet," he said, which was honest. He had one way of thinking that said the system was a machine that processed him, and another that said it was a relationship, imperfect and anxious on both ends, and he could not fully hold both at once. What he could do was stop refreshing. He closed the portal tab. He told himself he would check once a day, in the morning, and he wrote that at the bottom of the spreadsheet like a rule, knowing he might break it by Thursday.

He helped his mother put away the groceries, then went back upstairs and, instead of the portal, opened the essay he'd submitted, the one about his grandfather's workshop and how the old man built furniture in modules so that a dresser could travel in a van and be reassembled in a new apartment, modularity, his grandfather's word, which Logan had borrowed for the title. He read the last paragraph and found he still liked it. That was something that was his, regardless of what any committee projected onto a spreadsheet in a building he'd never see.

At nine, Zack texted a screenshot of his own portal, also unchanged, followed by: "tomorrow?" And Logan typed back "once a day, morning only," and put the phone face down on the desk beside the closed laptop, and went to brush his teeth.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries.
story:
The new warm-up was taped to the gym door by Tuesday, and by Wednesday half the team wanted it dead. It had diagrams. It had numbered phases. It had, in the bottom corner, a box labeled "coaching cues," as if a person could be cueled like a stagehand. Laurie stood in front of it with Kelsey and Ismail, all three of them still holding their backpacks, and read it aloud in the voice she used for funeral announcements.

"Hop and stick. Two minutes," she read. "Single-leg balance. Landing technique. Cutting drills." She lowered the paper. "It's prolix, is what it is. The old warm-up was three laps and a hamstring stretch and everybody lied about doing the stretch."

"First game is Friday," Ismail said, as if that settled it, which in a way it did. The coach had made it clear that Friday's roster depended on who ran the new routine all week, no exceptions, no negotiation. Kelsey kicked a basketball halfheartedly toward the rack and missed the rack. Nobody laughed, because everybody was thinking about Friday.

Laurie had a private reason to care, one she hadn't said out loud. Two winters ago she had sat in a hospital waiting room with her sister, who had planted her foot to change direction on a wet court and felt her knee give a sound like a knuckle cracking, louder. The surgeon had used the word "ligament" the way you'd say "Tuesday," and her sister had spent the spring learning to walk down stairs again, gripping the rail, swearing softly at each step. Laurie had been sixteen and useless, holding her sister's jacket. She remembered thinking, in the flat fluorescent light, that injuries were just weather, things that happened to you. She hadn't thought about whether anything could be done until the sheet appeared on the gym door.

The coach, who talked mostly in whistles, handed out a single-page summary and told them to read it themselves. That night Laurie collated the page with the diagrams from the door, spreading both on the kitchen table, matching phase numbers to stick figures, and found the sentence she'd skipped in the gym because Kelsey had been making fun of the word "stick." Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique, the sheet said, have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. She read it three times. Then she read it to her mother, who was peeling an orange and said, "So do the hopping, then," which was her mother's way of saying she was proud.

At Thursday's practice, the grumbling reached its operatic peak. Kelsey lay flat on the bleachers during the water break and announced that if she wanted to hop in place she would have joined a migratory bird. Ismail asked whether the word "stick" was a verb, an adjective, or a threat. Laurie stood in the middle of the key with her water bottle and held up one hand like a very short traffic officer.

"It says the ones that train balance and landing and cutting reduce knee ligament injuries," she said. "That's the whole point. That's why we're hopping."

"The whole point," Kelsey said from the bleachers, "is that my calves are dying."

"Your calves are dying for science."

"There's no science. There's a coach with a laminator."

Ismail sat up. "Is it real, though? The injury part?" He was the one on the team who had actually torn something, back in ninth grade, and he said it lightly, but he looked at Laurie the way you look at someone who might know. She thought of her sister's hand on the stair rail, the orange peel on the kitchen table, the sentence she had read three times. She also thought, honestly, that she didn't know whether hopping in place would save anyone's knees, only that it had been shown to reduce the risk, which was not the same as a promise, and she said so.

"It reduces the risk," she said. "It's not a force field. But my sister did the other thing, the laps and the lying about the stretch, and I watched her relearn stairs."

The gym went quiet in the way it does when a ball stops bouncing. Then Mr. Do, who taught chemistry down the hall and had been shooting free throws at the far basket with the proprietary air of a man who believed the gym was briefly his, called across the floor, "That was almost an epigram, Miss Laurie. Nearly quotable. Loses points for the stair part."

"That's the true part," Laurie called back.

"True things lose points all the time," said Mr. Do, and banked his free throw in.

They ran the warm-up at full effort that night, all phases, stick landings and everything, and Kelsey narrated her own suffering like a nature documentary, and Ismail counted his hops out loud in a fake accent, and Laurie jumped and stuck and jumped and stuck until her quads burned. Nobody's knee gave anything but the usual complaints. On Friday morning the roster went up on the gym door, taped over the diagrams, and Laurie walked toward it with Kelsey jostling her elbow and Ismail pretending not to run.

"If I'm cut," Kelsey said, "I'm blaming the laminator."

Laurie put her finger on the first name at the top of the page.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, US workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of $899, compared with $708 for those without one.
story:
The caps came out of the closet still smelling of the previous four years, which Hailey decided was either sentimental or a fire hazard. Her mother had commandeer the kitchen table for a graduation dinner, which meant the tablecloth with the wine stains from 2019 and a centerpiece made of lemons because someone had bought too many lemons. Yash was already at the door holding a card and a bag of tortilla chips he refused to explain. Laiba arrived eleven minutes later with her own cap, having graduated the day before at a different school across town, so the living room now contained two seniors and a growing suspicion that neither of them had thought past Saturday.

"Hailey," said her uncle, wedging himself between the lemons and the green bean casserole, "do you know what that diploma is worth?" He had the tone of a man about to reveal the location of buried treasure. "I looked it up. In 2023, workers twenty-five and over with a high school diploma had median weekly earnings of eight hundred ninety-nine dollars." He paused for effect. "Without one? Seven hundred and eight." He sat back like a lawyer resting his case.

"That's not a fortune," Yash said, crunching a chip.

"It's not a fortune," her uncle agreed, "but it's a difference, and differences add up." He passed the casserole with great ceremony, as though handing over the family savings.

Hailey laughed, but later, while everyone argued about whether the cake should be lemon-themed to match the centerpiece, she found herself doing the arithmetic on her phone under the table. A hundred ninety-one dollars a week. She typed it out, deleted it, typed it again. She had spent four years being told the diploma mattered, mostly by people who never said how, and here was a number, and the number was strangely small and strangely enormous at the same time. She could almost feel it settle into her like sedimentary layers, fact pressing down on fact, all the speeches and the assemblies compressed into one tidy weekly figure.

Laiba caught her at the dessert table. "Your uncle just monetized your childhood."

"He did it with citations," Hailey said. "That's the worst kind."

"You're going to college anyway. Why do you care what a diploma pays?"

"Because it's the first time anyone told me anything real about it." Hailey cut the cake into pieces of visibly different sizes and then rotated the plate so the biggest one faced her. "Everyone's either a cheerleader or an ideologue about education. Either it's the key to everything or it's a scam. Nobody ever just says, here's the number, it's decent, decide what you think."

Laiba stole the biggest piece anyway, rotating the plate back with the serenity of a professional. "So what do you think?"

"I think the number is true and it's also not the whole truth. It's median. Half the people are under it. It doesn't say anything about what the work is, or whether you can stand it." Hailey licked frosting off her thumb. "And I think I've been treating college like it's obvious, and the number made it less obvious, and I don't know if that's a good thing or an annoying thing."

Yash drifted over with his chip bag, now half mysterious. "Are you two having a crisis? At the cake?"

"An audit," said Laiba.

"A small one," Hailey said. "Self-directed."
